title: AI’s Risk to Financial Systems
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
Today’s AI agents have become exceptional hackers, and they’re already posing a threat to some of the most important infrastructure in modern life: banks
In both finance and tech, industry leaders are well aware of the dangers, and they’re gearing up for a fight

Earlier this year, as Anthropic prepared to release a powerful new model called Mythos, the firm gave an early preview of the AI to a select group of companies, aiming to help them shore up their defenses
JPMorganChase was on the list, and more banks were reportedly added as Anthropic expanded the program

After the rollout, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and then–Fed Chair Jerome Powell met with the heads of Bank of America, Citigroup, Goldman Sachs, and other major financial institutions to discuss the potential implications of the new model, which Anthropic claimed could “surpass all but the most skilled humans at finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities.” What makes AI agents different from past cybersecurity threats is that they move at machine speeds and can be summoned in groups
These bots can attack in swarms, hunting for cracks in companies’ back-end systems

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, which oversees many U.S. banks, wrote in a report to Congress this summer that AI has increased the “speed, scale, and sophistication of cyber-attacks targeting financial institutions.” Research from last year suggests that finance is likelier than other industries to face AI-enabled cyberattacks, but we can already see these threats playing out in the tech sector
Tech companies typically send out weekly software patches—updates and bug fixes, essentially—on what’s known as Patch Tuesday
In the age of agentic threats, the volume of those updates has ballooned
Microsoft patched nearly 1,000 issues earlier this month, an all-time record
The trend was accelerating before Mythos arrived, but, per J.P

Morgan’s analysis , the most advanced models have dramatically changed the cyber-risk landscape, leading to a “tsunami of patches.” Insiders have developed a word for it: “Patchmaggedon.” There’s also the risk that AI companies might lose control of the agents they send out into the world
Earlier this year, OpenAI revealed that its agents had defied instructions, breaching containment and hacking the servers of a company called Hugging Face
They also stole employee data and conspired to hide the evidence from their human managers

It was an incident that “exposed the speed of AI’s development,” as my colleague Josh Tyrangiel noted , “but also the lax oversight of the humans supposedly keeping tabs on it.” OpenAI has since disclosed several other lapses, and similar AI hacking incidents have occurred at Google , Anthropic , and Meta
What might happen if AI agents manage to identify substantial weaknesses in a bank’s code base? It’s hard to say with any certainty
But because banks underpin nearly every aspect of modern life, outages or disruptions to back-end systems could ripple across digital commerce
That some of the dangers associated with frontier AI are inherently unknowable can make preparing difficult

The companies building these tools don’t always understand the extent of a model’s capabilities until it’s been fully trained—OpenAI’s chief scientist has written that “AI is grown more than designed.” In spite of all this, the cybersecurity experts I spoke with made clear that the financial-services industry isn’t panicking
That’s in part because these agents and frontier models can also be used to prevent cyberattacks

Today’s engineers understand that defending against machine intelligence might itself require machine intelligence ; firms are already deploying these tools for fraud detection, risk management, and more

Mike Silverman, the head of strategy and innovation at the Financial Services Information Sharing and Analysis Center, told me that companies are using AI to beef up what’s known as anomaly detection—early-warning systems for potential threats—as well as other kinds of data monitoring

A cybersecurity executive at one of the largest banks in the United States told me that the industry’s Security Operations Centers—defense hubs traditionally managed by human beings—are exploring the possibility of developing their own agents, and that engineers across the sector are now designing systems with AI’s capabilities in mind
Because the financial sector has long been a target of scams, frauds, and data breaches, it’s already on high alert
But not every institution is equally capable of handling new threats; some smaller banks may lack the resources and security expertise of larger firms
As AI models advance, these tools may expose the difference between those who can afford to prepare for what’s coming, and those who can’t
Related: Assume you will be hacked, Matteo Wong writes
Deepfakes are coming for your bank account

Pezeshkian said Iran remained open to diplomacy to end the conflict

title: China Has No Use for AI Doomerism
excerpt: In Hangzhou, humanoid police robots wearing fluorescent-yellow vests patrol tourist hot spots, gently admonishing jaywalkers
body: In Hangzhou, humanoid police robots wearing fluorescent-yellow vests patrol tourist hot spots, gently admonishing jaywalkers

The Chinese AI chatbot Doubao is such a popular source of medical advice that citizens have begun to call the service “Doctor Doubao.” The authoritarian country is marshaling the state’s resources behind building a world-leading AI industry and pushing for the technology to be adopted across crucial sectors, including manufacturing, energy, and agriculture
Meanwhile, leaders are calling for a nationwide effort to nurture AI breakthroughs, adopting Cold War language last used when the country sought to develop a nuclear weapon

Encouraged by a steady drumbeat of state propaganda, the Chinese population has largely come to see AI, like previous waves of digital disruption, as a means of easing everyday life while also creating new jobs and industries

Polls indicate that the country is among the nations most excited about the prospects of AI, and doomers are tough to find. [ Read: What AI anxiety looks like in China ] So when the American tech sector reached a new level of AI panic last week, across the Pacific Ocean, the Chinese AI community largely shrugged—including the very people working on the technology’s safety

Chinese engineers and AI-safety experts I spoke with told me that although they recognize the existential safety risks of AI, they feel that losing control of the technology is a distinctly American challenge—for now
They’re far more preoccupied with catching up to U.S
AI models, which, despite the best efforts of Chinese companies such as DeepSeek and Moonshot AI, continue to lead in overall benchmarks

With the United States and China in a race to develop the most cutting-edge technologies, many in China also saw Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s proposal calling for an intentional slowdown in AI development as self-serving and driven by the geopolitical rivalry between the two countries
Amodei’s post, which fueled the AI panic across Silicon Valley, capped a whirlwind two months of cybersecurity breaches by agentic models from top U.S. and Chinese labs

It also attracted rare consensus from Amodei’s biggest rivals—OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and the SpaceXAI founder Elon Musk—and ignited a debate among industry executives, national-security hawks, and lawmakers
President Trump dismissed the warnings as a “SICK conspiracy,” while Republicans and Democrats clashed over proposed regulation
In China, the loudest voices commenting on the AI panic have come from state media and nationalist news commentators, who framed the outrage as just another ploy to delay China’s AI progress

Global Times , a state-owned media outlet run by the Chinese Communist Party, called the Anthropic executive’s warnings part of a “Cold War playbook” in a global AI race and singled out Amodei’s call for greater export controls to keep advanced chips out of China’s hands. “From the Chinese perspective, Dario’s proposal that China ‘pace the frontier’ seems hypocritical,” Kwan Yee Ng, an analyst at Concordia AI, a Beijing-based consultancy focused on AI safety, told me. “The country views itself as already being held back by the very export controls Amodei endorses.” The Chinese technology giant Huawei’s rotating chairperson, Xu Zhijun, told reporters that Chinese AI might not be powerful enough to encounter the same type of catastrophic safety risks that U.S. companies fear
Xu’s view is commonly held within the industry

One Chinese AI-software entrepreneur, who asked for anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the topic, told me that although cybersecurity is a constant concern, businesses are less concerned about losing control of AI models. “It’s so competitive here, and everyone is focused on bettering their own product
No one has the time to dwell on those issues,” he said
China is still playing catch-up, he added
If anyone’s going to lose control of AI first, he claimed, it will be the Americans
Another Chinese developer I spoke with who also asked for anonymity in order to speak openly, echoed the broader sense of AI optimism within China
A Stanford University industry report published this year cited polls showing that 84 percent of Chinese respondents said products and services that use AI made them excited
That’s compared with 53 percent of the global average, and 38 percent of people in the U.S
The developer told me that many of his peers tended to be “tech optimists” and didn’t subscribe to the same timelines for artificial general intelligence as Silicon Valley
Amodei’s warnings on AI misalignment are valuable insider signals, he said, but without more empirical evidence, it’s hard to get worked up
Part of the dismissive attitude is driven, it seems, by a broadly held suspicion of Amodei

The Anthropic CEO has repeatedly pushed for tight export controls to hold back China’s AI development and lobbied U.S. policy makers to clamp down on “unauthorized distillation” practices by major Chinese labs
That’s made him a controversial figure in the AI-developer community in China, despite the fact that Claude Code is widely used in the industry there

Last week, the DeepSeek engineer Liu Shengyu went viral on Chinese social media for a post that called on frontier AI to remain open and affordable, while also taking a personal shot at Amodei’s company

The prospect of Anthropic monopolizing the most advanced AI or AGI, Liu argued, was as severe as “Hitler acquiring atomic weapons before the Allies.” (Liu has since clarified that his views were personal and not representative of DeepSeek.) Another reason for the subdued reaction in China has to do with how AI companies there are structured
For the most part, they tend to be leaner and more resource-constrained than their U.S counterparts, which have teams devoted to long-term alignment and AI safety

To the extent that they have AI-safety resources, Chinese teams devote them to satisfying regulatory requirements, such as data security and filtering politically sensitive material. “The dynamics of AI safety is different in the U.S. and China,” Zilan Qian, a research scholar at GovAI, a think tank focused on helping governments navigate advanced AI, told me. “In the U.S., the labs and companies mainly drive the AI-safety discussion
In China, the government plays a central role in setting the AI-safety agenda and putting out regulation
Then the tech companies comply.” That’s not to say Chinese officials are completely unaware of AI risks
In recent months, multiple top Chinese politicians have sounded the alarm
Last week, Chen Yixin, the head of China’s state security agency, wrote in a public letter that AI was a serious threat to regime stability and required tighter scrutiny and control
And in July, President Xi Jinping warned about the risks of AI and pushed for multilateral cooperation in AI governance

China’s cyberspace regulator recently released an annual update of its AI Safety Governance Framework to include a hefty section about the risks from autonomous agents and the increased capabilities of frontier models
For all of the problems associated with America’s laissez-faire approach, China illustrates the opposite concern
Chinese officials worried about misinformation and losing control of the public discourse introduced some of the world’s tightest restrictions on the nascent technology
Generative-AI models in China are trained on data aligned with the party’s political ideology to ensure that the answers generated hold its worldview

title: How to Say ‘Stop Invading Greenland’ With Reindeer Sausage
excerpt: Food is like dance: a language, but not one you’d want to use in an emergency
body: Food is like dance: a language, but not one you’d want to use in an emergency

Food can say I love you or Congratulations (it helps if you are able to use icing on top of the food to make its message clearer) or even something slightly more subtle: I am proud of the seafood offerings of my region
It cannot say Look out! There is a projectile flying at your head! or Please stop trying to invade Greenland
Or can it? I went to “Taste of the Arctic” last week at the Danish ambassador’s residence to find out

The evening, billed as a celebration of “the culinary heritage and enduring cultural ties connecting Alaska, Greenland, and Denmark across the Arctic and North Atlantic,” came the week before the signing of an agreement about the U.S.’s presence in Greenland, though I am not sure I would have been able to tell you any details of the agreement being hashed out based on the available cuisine
The food was made by two chefs, Miki Siegsted and Joaquin Guzmán, representing Greenland and Denmark respectively
Guzmán, from Argentina, is the head chef of a Danish restaurant that cooks exclusively with Danish ingredients, meaning that if he wants chocolate, he cannot have chocolate
He has to engineer something like chocolate himself by using the by-products of beer brewing, which he reports have a delicious, chocolate-like flavor

Siegsted makes a point of introducing Greenlandic cuisine to a wider world, and is serving us reindeer sausage! (“Poor Rudolph,” says the waiter passing it around.) Fortunately, speeches let us know what the food is trying to tell us. “Food is one of the most honest languages we have,” Danish Ambassador Jesper Møller Sørensen says. “It tells you about a place, its water, its weather, and its people better than any briefing note could do.” He adds that “we have a very constructive dialogue with our American friends to achieve a framework that addresses the real security concerns that the United States has, that we share

But they are made easier and more human when we have them over a shared meal, rather than across a conference table.” Maybe we will find a little security framework in our salmon? Jacob Isbosethsen, of the Greenland delegation, says, “From hunting polar bears, reindeer, musk ox, whales, walruses, and seals to catching fish and birds, our relationship with nature has always been deeply connected to our way of life.” However, the chefs will not be serving “most of the proteins or animals I mentioned earlier.” But we will still get to enjoy other arctic delights, the product of “56,000 people on the world’s largest island” with the “most modern shrimp-fishing fleet in the Arctic.” Senator Lisa Murkowski acknowledges that “some will say, well, I don’t know, when I think about the Arctic, I don’t think about really exotic or great foods or Michelin-starred restaurants,” but she is not included in that misguided “some.” “When you begin with honest, incredible seafood that comes from these cold waters, you can make just about anything fabulous.” The speeches also have the effect of postponing any access to these flavors until almost 8 p.m

Having made the unacceptable rookie mistake of thinking that, at an evening event at an embassy themed around food, there would be enough food for dinner, served at dinnertime, I am quite hungry and (after a Hygge In a Can) perhaps excessively convivial. (This shows how little time I spend going to Events at Embassies, which is why I never know what is Really Happening in Washington.) I post myself in front of the two tasting stations like a ravenous anteater squatting outside an anthill, or, to use a more arctic animal, a polar bear resting on an ice floe

I do such a good job of this that I entirely deny a man access to reindeer sausage! The parade of arctic food runs the gamut from one seafood to another seafood to the first seafood again, but fermented this time

The seafood is fresh and delicious! The reindeer sausage is maybe the best sausage I’ve ever eaten in my life? It tastes like a Slim Jim, if that Slim Jim were gourmet and assembled by Santa under desperate circumstances
I should preface all of my descriptions of food by saying: Once, I had the enormous privilege of getting to visit Sicily with my in-laws
The waiter brought me the hot, pillowycrusted pizza with melted cheese and mouth-watering sausage on board (“on board”? Already my descriptive powers are flagging) and set it in front of me
I devoured several slices. “This tastes like DiGiorno!” I exclaimed
I was trying to compliment the pizza, but my in-laws were horrified
This is why I am a humor columnist and not a food critic
All right, now that you are warned, on to Taste of the Arctic
My favorite taste of the Arctic was the reindeer sausage, by a mile

There was a mustard sauce on top, and the sausage engaged in a sort of dialogue with it over the course of the bite (I am trying to describe the food! How do you think it’s going so far?), saying things like, I am spicy! to which the sausage responded, You think you are the only thing that is spicy? I, too, am spicy! Diplomatically, I have no idea how this translates
It arrived in a little boat, as though it were ready to row out in Greenland’s defense, should it be called to

It tasted like lox on a cucumber, but with, I think, a hint of citrus? There was also something called a cod-and-salmon ballotine, where cod (white) and salmon (pink) were curled together into a small dumpling and garlanded with a green sauce so that it looked like an edible Italian flag
Unclear what the diplomatic significance of this was
Should Italy be more involved in the Arctic? This tasted like salty mashed potatoes, which is a compliment
I also tried salmon with salmon eggs on top, and a sort of brown crumble
A WHOLE FISH FAMILY PERISHED AT MY BEHEST! And I would do it again
I wrote in my notes that there was “guacamole” on this, but I think I was mistaken
Maybe it was the Danish equivalent of guacamole, made from lingonberry leaves or something
The one thing I’ll say about the food at Taste of the Arctic is that there was not enough of it

These dishes were all bite-size, the kind of thing a mouse would lug home to his family, who would then say, in a disappointed tone, “But you said you were bringing dinner for all of us.” At one point, I perched forlornly at the edge of the tasting tables
Their white, empty tablecloths with no food on them evoked the arctic tundra, frozen, empty of food for the winter
Perhaps deliberately? The strange thing about this event was not the food, which was delicious
Or the Hygge-inspired beer, which was excellent
Or the fact that the Danish ambassador’s residence was hospitable and full of bicycles, which it also was
What was odd was that we were in a geopolitical situation where this diplomacy via cod and reindeer innards felt warranted at all

What was odd were those harrowing months when it looked as though the president wanted to annex Greenland, destroying our relationship with Denmark and ending the post–World War II international liberal order

If your president goes rogue and decides that he wants to annex Greenland because the Mercator projection makes it look impressively big, or because he thinks the United States is not cold enough on average (I guess that’s one solution to climate change!), it is not the fault of the honest, incredible seafood
But when the going gets tough, the tough serve shellfish
Denmark and Greenland are both party to it, and it will allow us to build bases there, which we already do, and have “undersea access,” which, based on the tastiness of the cod, is important

title: The Makings of a Prewar World
excerpt: Donald Trump offered perhaps the clearest summation yet of his worldview in an otherwise discursive address to the United Nations General Assembly yesterday
body: Donald Trump offered perhaps the clearest summation yet of his worldview in an otherwise discursive address to the United Nations General Assembly yesterday

Defending the American takeover of Venezuelan oil, he invoked an old maxim: “To the victor belongs the spoils.” He then presented Iran with a choice between accepting his terms and being driven “into hell with no chance of survival.” These remarks are the latest sign that world politics is entering an era when might makes right
Yet Trump is only one of the leaders driving this rupture from the post–World War II international order
Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have also broken the order, although their methods differ profoundly—morally, legally, and otherwise
American policy may change when Trump leaves office in January 2029, but Putin and Xi may remain in power well into the next decade
A new American president will likely not be able to restore the old order or create a better one, even if they want to
Their greatest challenge will be to arrest the slide
International order is a notoriously vague and politically contested concept
Many leaders in the global South, along with Western critics, reject the idea that the United States ever consistently abided by a rules-based system
They point to Western military interventions, double standards, and the unequal distribution of power within international institutions
But the old order’s failures do not mean that its restraints were meaningless

In his first book, A World Restored , Henry Kissinger argued that a stable and legitimate order rests on a limited consensus: an understanding among the major powers about what he called the permissible aims and methods of foreign policy
Governments can compete intensely and violate rules without seeking to overturn the system itself

The danger arises when a major power becomes so dissatisfied with the limits imposed upon it that it adopts a revolutionary foreign policy. [ Vivian Salama: America’s allies are no longer waiting for Trump to leave ] Under the old international order, major powers did not, as a general rule, conquer and annex the territory of their neighbors
The global trading system was based on reciprocity, tariffs were historically low, and markets were relatively open

And, although it was the world’s strongest country, the United States exercised enough self-discipline to allow its allies to grow into genuine partners, not vassals to be constantly squeezed for concessions
Over the past decade, and decisively since the pandemic, that consensus about permissible conduct has collapsed
Putin launched the largest war in Europe since World War II with his invasion of Ukraine in 2022
He more than anyone has revived the idea that countries can expand their borders through the use of force
Combined Russian- and Ukrainian-military casualties (those killed, wounded, and missing) have reached approximately 2 million people
European governments have accused Russia of an expanding campaign of sabotage, cyberattacks, arson, and drone incursions below the threshold of conventional war

North Korea has intervened directly in this war, and many other nations are indirectly involved—China and Iran on the side of Russia; Europe, the United States (at least under Joe Biden), and Asian democracies on the side of Ukraine
Under Xi, China has broken the global trading system
Xi has used the power of the Chinese state to establish dominance in advanced manufacturing, reduce China’s imports as much as possible, and aggressively grow its exports
The result is that China has enormous excess capacity
Its goods flood into the rest of the world at prices impossible to compete with, leaving other countries to choose between deindustrialization and protectionism
More and more of them are selecting the latter
This policy is not as morally egregious as Putin’s invasion of Ukraine, but it has toppled a key pillar of the international economic order
Since taking office for a second term, in 2025, Trump has turned American power against U.S. allies and partners

He imposed the highest tariffs in nearly a century on Canada, Japan, South Korea, India, and the European Union and used the threat of more to extract hundreds of billions of dollars in investment pledges
He mused about making Canada the 51st state and seizing Greenland
He pushed Ukraine to sign over a share of its mineral wealth in the middle of a war for its national survival
Under Trump, the United States sees itself not as the guarantor of an alliance system of like-minded democracies, but as a dominant power that wields its influence for singular, transactional gain
Trump has broken the restraint that made American primacy tolerable to most of the rest of the world
Reports suggest that he may meet Xi and Putin for a “big three” trilateral on the margins of the Asia Pacific Economic Summit in Shenzhen in November, which could mark the formal end of the old order
The rupture has produced an international environment that feels ever more like that of a prewar period
This does not mean that a major conflict is inevitable
But if one occurs, future historians will not find its causes sudden or mysterious
They are in plain sight. [ Listen: Trump battles against an economy of his making ] The major powers are building up their militaries and racing to master drone warfare and artificial intelligence
Trump’s lack of commitment to alliances, especially in Europe, raises the prospect that an aggressor may calculate that it can act without triggering much of a U.S. reaction

title: A Revealing Exchange Between Donald Trump and Kaitlan Collins
excerpt: When CNN’s Kaitlan Collins approached President Trump with a question about the Iran war at the United Nations General Assembly yesterday, the president scolded
body: When CNN’s Kaitlan Collins approached President Trump with a question about the Iran war at the United Nations General Assembly yesterday, the president scolded her for being there at all. “I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me,” Trump said, adding, “You should not be here covering me.” Presumably, he said this because CNN is among the three outlets , along with MS NOW and Politico , that Trump has barred from White House grounds because he didn’t like their coverage
But, to state the obvious, the United Nations is not the White House
If a journalist is denied a press pass from one entity, she’s not precluded from getting credentialed by another

As Collins said to Trump, “The United Nations allowed us in, sir.” The exchange highlights Trump’s warped understanding of journalism—in which stories are either good or bad, reporters are “ friendly ” or “ terrible ,” and a president decides who covers him and who doesn’t. “There’s something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories,” he said when he banned CNN and the other two outlets. “Now, if they want to write them, that’s fine
But I don’t have to let them into my—into the people’s house.” As Trump noted when he corrected himself, the White House serves the American people—but so does the press

Since the days of FDR, a cadre of rotating print, TV, and radio reporters have traveled with the president wherever he goes, including on weekends and holidays, to provide an unbroken and independent record of everything the president says and does in public
This press pool exists because not every reporter can constantly trail the president; neither can every citizen

Political reporters stand in for people who want to know what their most important elected representative is doing, but who have day jobs. [ Read: President Piggy ] The importance of the pool became especially visible this week when, in solidarity, the other four networks that typically share pool duties with CNN—ABC, CBS, Fox News, and NBC— suspended their pool coverage of the president

This led to an unintentionally Veep -like moment during Trump’s unveiling of his new helipad, when no networks provided audio as Trump appeared flanked by smiling construction workers, speaking without sound. (A Newsmax host gingerly described the scene as a sign that the CNN ban was perhaps “backfiring just a little bit.”) Trump has a long history with the press—and of seeming not to understand how it works. (As with many things pertaining to the president, however, determining whether his ignorance is genuine or strategic can be difficult.) At times, he has appeared to feign confusion in an effort to get reporters to do what he wants

In a 1997 New Yorker profile , for instance, Trump repeatedly told the reporter following him that his words were “off the record, but you can use it”—guidance that makes no sense, because “off the record” is an agreement that means a reporter can’t use a piece of information in a story

When he was campaigning for president in 2016, Trump frequently railed against “libel laws” and promised to “loosen them up” but struggled to describe what that meant. (“I’d have to get my lawyers in to tell you,” he told The Washington Post .) He suggested that late-night comedians should devote “equal time” to jokes about Democrats and his administration, seemingly invoking a law that doesn’t apply to either presidents or late-night jokes. [ Read: The press is not the root of Trump’s problems ] A fact that seems to bedevil Trump most is that the press doesn’t take orders from him, and that therefore almost every reporter he encounters will at some point seem “unfriendly.” In his current term, one of Trump’s first orders of business was to decree that the White House would choose the reporters in the press pool, breaking with the tradition of news organizations choosing

He’s trying to ban the Associated Press from parts of the White House because the wire service continues to refer, against Trump’s wishes, to the body of water south of the United States as “the Gulf of Mexico.” Trump regularly interrogates pool reporters about which network they’re really with, and dubs the answer “fake news” if it’s not one that he likes

As evidenced by the exchange at the United Nations, CNN’s Collins seems to provoke his disdain to an unusual degree: Over the years, Trump has attempted to bar her from White House press events, tried to make her sit in the back of the press room, called her “ stupid ” and “ nasty ,” implored her to smile , and told her she should be ashamed of herself because she used to be “a conservative from Alabama.” To which Collins replied, “I’m still from Alabama, sir.” Presidents have always had testy relations with the press, of course, and have tried to minimize negative coverage
The behavior of Trump’s administration, however, often shades into something more sinister
His FBI raided the home of a Washington Post reporter whose coverage he found objectionable, and Trump has sued and defunded news organizations whose coverage he deemed biased

MS NOW reported in May that the FBI had opened a criminal investigation focusing on my colleague Sarah Fitzpatrick, related to an article she wrote about FBI Director Kash Patel. (The FBI has denied the existence of such an investigation.) As a reporter, I spend a lot of time explaining to sources—many of whom have never interacted with the media—the basics of journalism: that we don’t accept or grant payment for interviews, that reporters don’t interact with advertisers, and that most mainstream outlets pride themselves on not affiliating with any given political ideology

Some degree of media illiteracy is understandable at a time when thousands of local newspapers have closed , and when influencers—some of whom secretly accept payment for their branded videos—compete for attention on social media with journalists reporting the truth
Journalists shouldn’t have to explain their jobs, though, to someone who has lived his entire adult life in the public eye, and who is now America’s most important public servant
But as Collins showed at the UN, apparently, they must.

title: How to Argue in the Trump Era Without Losing Your Mind

body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with his reaction to the shooting at the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Ontario on Yom Kippur
David discusses the rise of violence against Jews around the world, and why condemnations of anti-Semitic violence ring hollow when they come from people who spread myths about Jewish conspiracies
Then, David is joined by Jessica Tarlov, the co-host of The Five on Fox News and the Raging Moderates podcast
They talk about her new book, I Disagree: Winning Arguments Without Losing Friends , and how her upbringing helped shape her ability to disagree cordially
David and Jessica also discuss when to debate someone versus when to ignore them so as not to give them a platform
Finally, David ends the show with a review of the novel Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke
The following is a transcript of the episode: David Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show
I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic
My guest this week will be Jessica Tarlov, co-host of the Fox News program The Five and author of the new book I Disagree: Winning Arguments Without Losing Friends
She’s also the co-host with Scott Galloway of the Raging Moderates podcast
The book for discussion this week will be a much-acclaimed new novel, Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke, and I’ll be discussing that at the bottom of the program

But before either my dialogue with Jessica Tarlov or the book discussion of Yesteryear , I wanna open with some thoughts about an outrage that happened in a place very close to me, just this, these past days
On the Jewish holiday of Yom Kippur, the most holy day of the Jewish year, a gunman opened fire on the synagogue in this Canadian town, the Ontario town of Belleville

Many of the details of this incident remain a little murky, but what we do have is: The alleged gunman, the apparent gunman, is in hospital, and so is a police officer who gallantly came to the rescue of the synagogue
None of the worshippers in the synagogue were injured
The alleged gunman apparently used a shotgun, which discharged a lot of pellets, did a lot of physical damage, but it was not the kind of high-powered rifle that would’ve shot up this building
This story has become a big story in Ontario, in Canada, and around the world
It is one of a many of a long series of incidents of intensifying violence against Jewish worshippers all around the world since October 7th of 2023
To read about it in Belleville is very striking, however, and not just because it’s so close to me
I have worshipped at the synagogue, Sons of Jacob Synagogue, where the crime took place
I see this street in my mind, and it’s such a powerful symbol of how life has changed for North American Jews
The Sons of Jacob Synagogue is a congregation that dates back to the early 20th century, but the building was built in the middle 1950s
It’s a piece of modernist architecture, quite small, and it faces directly on a road in a residential neighborhood
There are no security precautions other than a locked door, because it was built at a time when it never occurred to the Jews of North America that they could face violence from their neighbors
That kind of threat was something they remembered, but from across the ocean and from a different time, not here and not now
But, of course, it is here, and it is now
And it is striking all over the continent, all over the world

When these kinds of incidents happen, a certain kind of speaker, a certain kind of politician, a certain kind of online influencer, a certain kind of journalist will say, It is very important not to conflate the Jews of here— wherever “here” is, Ontario and Canada, the United States, New York, wherever it is— with the Jews over there
We should not be blaming the Jews of Belleville for the crimes of the state of Israel
Now this kind of remark is intended to be a defense of the Jewish community that is under attack, but it is, in its own way, a form of incitement

Because when you say we must not conflate the Jews here with the Jews there, we must not blame our Jews for those Jews, what you’re doing is suggesting that there are some Jews who deserve the kind of violence just that happened
And what you’re also doing is offering safety to certain Jews on condition that they disavow others
We see a lot of this in remarks by some people who are disaffiliated Jews, who will say, We can be safer if only we separate ourselves from the Jews in Israel who are under attack
I hear that, and I think that that is the counsel of cowardice
To buy safety for yourself by abandoning others, by separating yourself from others who equally deserve safety, that seems to me a reprehensible thing
But as a strictly factual matter, it’s just wrong
That the no-conflation argument— Don’t attack the Jews here for what the Jews over there did —begins with the foundation upon a lie

And the lie is the lie that we are hearing again and again that Israel committed genocide, that is, Nazi-like atrocities, in its war of self-defense that began when it was attacked so atrociously on October 7th, 2023

I once made it a project to dig back through the archives to find who was the first person who compared the state of Israel to the Nazis, and when did it happen? And as best I can tell, the first, or the first prominent person, to do it was the British historian Arnold Toynbee, who makes the point in a book published in 1954, the eighth volume of his Study of History
Within six years of the independence of the state of Israel, Arnold Toynbee is publishing a comparison of the state of Israel to the Nazis

title: A congressional representative just proposed killing America’s border tower program
excerpt: Delia Ramirez, a Democratic US representative from Illinois, has announced a plan to introduce new legislation to terminate the surveillance tower program along
body: Delia Ramirez, a Democratic US representative from Illinois, has announced a plan to introduce new legislation to terminate the surveillance tower program along the US southern border.  The announcement comes just days after publication of an MIT Technology Review investigation, “Dying on Camera,” in which we looked at deaths along the border that took place close to one or more of these towers
MIT Technology Review found that nearly one in four deaths we analyzed between 2015 and early 2026 occurred within their advertised range

We also showed that the Department of Homeland Security does not keep track of these deaths or other metrics on the towers’ success or failure.  Ramirez, who sits on the Homeland Security Committee, cited MIT Technology Review ’s reporting that nearly “1,100 people have died within range of a billion-dollar surveillance tower system between 2015 and 2026,” adding, “The towers that we have paid a billion dollars to just don’t work.”  The legislation, the Reimagining Safety Act, was developed in consultation with community groups and local and state representatives

The advocacy organizations Just Futures Law, which focuses on immigrant rights and racial justice, and Mijente, which describes itself as a “vehicle for building independent Latinx political power,” helped shape the calls to terminate the border towers program, following a joint report they put out earlier this year on the technology used by ICE.  The legislation is intended to be part of a broader proposal to replace the Department of Homeland Security with a new Department of Community Safety while moving CISA, FEMA, TSA, and customs functions to other existing federal agencies

Her office has yet to release the text of the proposed legislation, saying that it will come in the next few weeks.  There has been growing public support for abolishing ICE in the wake of the second Trump administration’s highly visible enforcement operations across American cities, the buildout of its detention apparatus, and shootings by ICE and CBP agents
Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a delivery driver, was shot in the back by an ICE agent just last weekend in Austin, Texas.  But for Ramirez, abolishing just ICE is not enough
At a press conference held in Chicago on Wednesday, Ramirez said, “There’s no question that DHS has to be dismantled
We need to provide them a road map in how we do it,” Ramirez said
It will not be the first time that a bill to dismantle the Department of Homeland Security has been introduced, but previous proposals have not gone very far

This proposal will also face a steep uphill battle in Congress, where even some Democrats favor reforming rather than outright dismantling the organization.  Ramirez, however, sits on both the House committee that oversees the department, and is the ranking member on the Homeland Security Committee’s cybersecurity subcommittee.   “We’re limiting state surveillance, we’re reigning unlawful abuses of data and curbing the militarized enforcement
We’re beginning the process of establishing a separate civil immigration system,” Ramirez said
DHS and CBP did not offer an immediate response for comment.

title: The Download: India’s smart glasses menace and AI’s trillion-dollar gamble
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology

Smart glasses are already causing havoc in India When Shubnam saw an Instagram video of a Delhi protest they had attended, they realized a content creator wearing Meta smart glasses had recorded them surreptitiously
The mocking reel drew millions of views, along with transphobic abuse and AI-generated memes
Experts warn that many others will experience similar ordeals as smart glasses go mainstream
The risks are particularly acute in India, where covert recording and the circulation of images without consent are already pervasive
The bigger issue is that the smart glasses aren’t just being used to turn ordinary people into targets of viral “pranks.” They’re also becoming a tool of police surveillance

Here’s why smart glasses are creating new privacy risks in India . —Anuj Behal MIT Technology Review Narrated: what’s at stake in AI’s trillion-dollar gamble When Jessica Wachter, a University of Pennsylvania finance professor, wanted to assess AI’s impact on the economy over the next few years, she started with a simple fact: a handful of so-called hyperscalers are investing huge amounts of money to build AI data centers

Instead of trying to predict how widely deployed AI models will be, Wachter asked how fast the hyperscalers’ earnings will need to grow to justify their spending through 2027, when expenditures are expected to reach nearly $1.1 trillion
AI companies will need to achieve an extraordinary increase in productivity just to break even by 2030
This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts
Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released

The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 Hackers claim they’ve stolen data on almost all FBI employees The ShinyHunters group says it seized more than 2 TB of data. ( Axios ) + Including agents’ names, addresses, and phone numbers. ( 404 Media ) + ShinyHunters says the attack was retaliation for an FBI alert. ( Reuters $) + Now is a good time for doing crime. ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 Anthropic and OpenAI have both released lower-cost models They face growing competition from cheaper Chinese models. ( CNBC ) + Startups have been reducing their reliance on the two labs. ( Bloomberg $) + The new models are the first since their calls for an AI slowdown. ( FT $) + Their CEOs are set to brief the UN Security Council today. ( Quartz ) + Could AI really kill us all? ( MIT Technology Review ) 3 Trump’s Treasury chief could soon become his new AI czar Scott Bessent has played a central role in US-China AI talks. ( Semafor ) + Other contenders include Michael Kratsios and Scott Kupor. ( Gizmodo ) + Will Trump’s AI rebrand to “superintelligence” catch on? ( BBC ) 4 Scientists are turning renewable electricity directly into food The goal is to make more food with less land. ( New Scientist $) + Companies are creating food out of thin air. ( MIT Technology Review ) 5 A “fire amoeba” has broken the heat survival record for complex life The newly discovered organism can grow and reproduce at 63°C. ( NPR ) + It could inform the search for life elsewhere. ( New Scientist $) 6 Meta quietly tested a “human concierge” for its Muse AI agent Contractors secretly handled some calls placed by Muse. ( Reuters $) + Staff raised concerns about privacy and misleading users. ( 404 Media ) 7 Data centres are replacing copper with light to cut energy use Photonics can move data with less heat than electrical wiring. ( BBC ) + Virtual power plants could also help. ( MIT Technology Review ) 8 AI models built from rat brains just got closer to reality AWS is tapping rat neurons to make video AI faster. ( Wired $) 9 Uber is betting on human drivers to give its robotaxis an edge They can cover demand spikes while autonomous cars recharge. ( Axios ) 10 A humanoid robot took on an amateur fighter in a cage The brief bout was billed as the first human-robot MMA fight. ( Futurism ) Quote of the day “The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake

It’s not fake; it’s actually amazing.” —President Donald Trump tells the UN General Assembly why he wants to rename AI “superintelligence.”  One more thing COURTESY OF PAINCHEK AI is changing how we quantify pain At Orchard Care Homes, nurses used to rely on an observational scale to assess pain in residents who couldn’t communicate verbally
But agitated residents were sometimes assumed to have behavioral issues, while their pain went untreated
Then, in 2021, the care-home chain began trialing PainChek, a smartphone app that scans a resident’s face for microscopic muscle movements and uses AI to output a pain score
Within weeks, the pilot unit saw fewer prescriptions and calmer corridors
Now researchers are racing to turn pain into something a camera or sensor can score as reliably as blood pressure

But when algorithms measure our suffering, does that change how we understand and treat it? Discover how AI is changing the way we assess pain . —Deena Mousa We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .) + Scientists have discovered the first new penguin species in more than 100 years. + Discover the filmmaking skills that made Paul Verhoeven’s RoboCop a directing masterclass . + What happens when fast food meets local tastes? These unusual international menu items offer some tasty answers. + Dance to every track the crowd has identified at Berghain since 2024 with this media player , which replays each night in sequence.

title: Smart glasses are already causing havoc in India
excerpt: Covert recording, real consequences: When a content creator filmed a 38-year-old transfeminine graphic designer at a Delhi protest using Meta smart glasses, the
body: Covert recording, real consequences: When a content creator filmed a 38-year-old transfeminine graphic designer at a Delhi protest using Meta smart glasses, the resulting viral reel drew millions of views and a torrent of transphobic abuse—undoing, in Shubnam's words, "two decades of progress" overnight

A safeguard that isn't: Meta's recording indicator light—its primary privacy protection—can be physically disabled or covered, with tutorials and even a market for "stealth mode" modifications already circulating online

Police are using them too: Delhi police used Meta smart glasses to film student protesters for weeks this summer, allegedly threatening to send footage to their parents and universities—while the courts dismissed the students' complaints as "luxury litigation." The law can't keep up: India's voyeurism statutes were written for more obvious violations, leaving little recourse when someone is filmed in public and humiliated at scale—and platforms have up to 36 hours to act, long enough for harmful footage to spread beyond recall. " data-chronoton-post-id="1144953" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Shubnam was packing boxes for a move into a new home when their friend sent them an Instagram video

The footage had only been up for a few hours, but it was days old, recorded at a Delhi protest this spring against a bill that would have narrowed the legal recognition for transgender people in India
There, a content creator known for rage-bait videos had approached Shubnam, a 38-year-old transfeminine graphic designer and educator
Shubnam, who uses a single chosen name, was dressed in a green sari with a shaved head, and the creator asked why they were wearing “female clothing.” Shubnam told him to back off

Only when the video arrived did they realize he had recorded the exchange on Meta smart glasses, styled to look like ordinary Wayfarers.  Edited into a mocking reel, the footage drew millions of views, along with transphobic abuse, reaction videos, and AI-generated memes
It spread from Instagram to X and YouTube

Copies remain online today.  For Shubnam, the video has caused huge harm. “All it took was one unconsented video to rewind two decades of progress that I made all on my own,” they told MIT Technology Review . “For a moment, it felt like this entire adult life I had lived was just a long lucid dream, and I was going to wake up as that clueless queer child again.” They haven’t worn a sari outside their neighborhood since
Experts warn that many others will experience similar ordeals as smart glasses go mainstream
And they say privacy problems are becoming especially acute in India, where covert recording and the circulation of images without consent are already pervasive
Cases of cyberstalking, sextortion, deepfakes, and other forms of online abuse are growing in the country

And the chances of a crackdown on technologies such as smart glasses are slim, given that Indian law enforcement authorities are themselves increasingly adopting AI-powered surveillance tools, including facial recognition systems and their own AI-enabled smart glasses
An unequal burden Smart glasses are among the fastest-growing devices in India’s wearables market, according to the International Data Corporation , a research firm

And Reliance Jio, one of the country’s largest telecommunications companies, says that later this year it’s set to launch a sub-$105 rival to Meta’s glasses, the latest model of which have a $420 price tag in India.  The core privacy issue is that these cameras don’t look like cameras, so targets may not notice they’re being recorded

Yet Meta rejects the idea that it’s responsible for protecting people from intrusions, says Janusz Świerczyński, an Oxford Saïd Business School researcher who studies privacy and emerging technology. “More and more, the expectation is being placed on bystanders to look out for themselves,” he says
That means it’s up to them to spot a small LED in the glasses frames that activates when recording is in progress
Meta also relies on wearers to behave responsibly, says Świerczyński
Reliance Jio did not respond to our request for comment on privacy issues related to its upcoming glasses
Creators have already demonstrated ways to circumvent the recording light on Meta’s glasses
Tutorials show users how to cover or otherwise obscure the LED while continuing to record

Back in March, Wired documented a market for “stealth mode” modifications that physically disable the light or remove it entirely.  All that makes covert recording easier, and the risks are not borne equally. Świerczyński says women and other marginalized groups face greater harm when inconspicuous devices capture and circulate footage without consent—as happened to Shubnam

The bigger problem, however, is that in India smart glasses aren’t just being used to turn ordinary people into targets of viral “pranks.” They’re also being adopted as a tool of police surveillance.  In June, when thousands of young demonstrators gathered to protest problems with the country’s education system, Delhi police used Meta smart glasses to record them

In fact, a petition filed by former Jawaharlal Nehru University Students’ Union president Aishe Ghosh before the Delhi High Court alleged that police had filmed protesters continuously for weeks, including while they were eating and resting
It also alleged that the police had threatened to send footage of student demonstrators to their parents and colleges

In July, India’s solicitor general dismissed the case in court as “ luxury litigation. ” Instead of investigating the students’ complaints, police turned on the students themselves, opening 10 criminal investigations for offenses including rioting, assault on public servants, and damage to public property

Some of the protesters, who spoke to MIT Technology Review on condition of anonymity, say they never saw the LED on the Meta AI glasses police wore during the demonstrations.  Filming without consent Meta maintains that its safeguard works

The company told MIT Technology Review , “Every pair has a capture LED that blinks when you take a photo or video that you can save or share; it can’t be turned off, and if someone covers or damages the LED, the camera is disabled.” The company also says users are responsible for complying with the law and respecting people’s privacy

That approach is risky, especially in India, where norms around filming and consent are still highly disputed and digital literacy is still uneven, says Sameer Parmar, a counselor at Meri Trustline, a safety partner working with Meta and YouTube to support people harmed by online content.  “The hardware is improving, but the country’s weak understanding of consent gives an invisible camera far more room to cause harm,” he says
Simply being in a public place is often treated as implicit consent to be photographed or filmed

He says the help line has been seeing an uptick in cases involving covert recording and nonconsensual footage. “Violations of this access have increased significantly and are expected to rise further in India,” he says
People are recorded in medical settings, during private encounters, and in public spaces
Those with less power to object are particularly vulnerable, he adds. “It’s either trolling or it’s playing pranks on them and then recording them” he says

Abusers “do target people who are a little more unaware or susceptible to how this technology-facilitated harm works.” The law in India has not caught up with this new kind of harm, says Apar Gupta, a lawyer and founder-director of the Internet Freedom Foundation. “India’s laws against voyeurism and the sharing of intimate images were designed largely around more recognizable forms of abuse,” he says, citing offenses such as secretly filming someone undressing, using a toilet, or engaged in a sexual act. “[The laws] offer limited protection when someone is secretly filmed in an ordinary public setting and the footage is then used to humiliate them,” he says

Social media platforms’ rules do offer another route to removing harmful content filmed with smart glasses, but it’s not an immediate remedy. “Under India’s current rules, platforms can have up to 36 hours to act on certain complaints—a window that can be long enough for a video to be downloaded, copied, and circulated elsewhere,” he says
The problem of filming without consent seems set to grow

According to the Financial Times , some internal prototypes of new Meta glasses include AI features that continuously photograph and listen to the wearer’s surroundings, enabling the glasses to later recall what they saw or heard
These functions wouldn’t activate the external recording indicator, making it impossible for bystanders to know when information about them is being collected
Meta told us it intends to keep the LED for active capture, such as taking photos or recording video, but not for AI features that interpret the wearer’s surroundings
Its argument is that a constantly blinking light could eventually become so commonplace that people stop noticing it

title: Mosque attack highlights evolving extremism landscape that has brought Pakistan-Afghanistan ties to crisis point
url:
<title>Mosque attack highlights evolving extremism landscape that has brought Pakistan-Afghanistan ties to crisis point</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761742/original/file-20260923-50-u2vqxy.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=149%2C182%2C5239%2C3493&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Security forces inspect the site of a blast at a mosque in Kohat, Pakistan, on Sept. 18, 2026. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/security-officials-inspect-the-site-of-a-blast-at-a-mosque-news-photo/2295294550?adppopup=true">Hussain Ali/Anadolu via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The suicide bombing and gun attack that <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/18/bomb-attack-at-pakistan-mosque-kills-at-least-15-injures-50">killed dozens in northwest Pakistan</a> on Sept. 18, 2026, highlighted the fragile security situation in the South Asian country. But it also shone a light on the complex and evolving extremism landscape there and the strained relationship between Pakistan and neighboring Afghanistan.</p>

<p>The assault took place as worshipers gathered for Friday prayers in the city of Kohat, in Khyber Puktunkhwa province, northwest Pakistan. A suicide bomber rammed an explosives-laden car through the wall of a <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/19/world/asia/pakistan-mosque-attack-bahadur.html">police complex</a> in the city of Kohat, targeting the mosque inside. Gunmen then exchanged fire with law enforcement officials during a 20-hour standoff. In all, <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/death-toll-31-pakistan-police-compound-attack-afp-reports-2026-09-19/">31 people were killed</a>, including 16 police officers, while over <a href="https://www.dawn.com/news/2030862">100 people</a> were reported injured.</p>

<p>Supporters of the militant group <a href="https://jamestown.org/rise-and-growing-threat-of-ittehad-ul-mujahideen-pakistan/">Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan</a>, or IMP, claimed responsibility on encrypted apps like Telegram. But other seemingly aligned groups distanced themselves from the attack. Pakistan responded by <a href="https://www.dw.com/en/pakistan-says-strikes-in-afghanistan-killed-28-terrorists/a-79350604">conducting airstrikes in Afghanistan</a>, home to at least one of the gunmen.</p>

<p><iframe id="9W4eJ" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/9W4eJ/2/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A map of the Afghanistan-Pakistan border"></iframe></p>

<p>Over the past two years, <a href="https://www.clemson.edu/cbshs/about/profiles/index.html?userid=ajadoon">we have conducted</a> <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=FA7fDloAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">fieldwork in this region</a> and closely monitored the operational and propaganda activity of violent extremist groups, including the IMP. The attack and its fallout reveal much about the state of collaboration and friction among the various militant entities that have fueled violence.</p>

<h2>Who is Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan?</h2>

<p>The IMP is a jihadist coalition formed in April 2025 from three smaller militant factions: Lashkar-e-Islam, the Hafiz Gul Bahadur Group and Inqilab-e-Islami Pakistan.</p>

<p>By late 2025, it had become the most active jihadist group in Pakistan after the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan, also referred to as the Pakistani Taliban.</p>

<p>The IMP’s main objectives appear to be weakening the Pakistani state through attacks on police and security forces and advancing Islamist rule. Its operations are largely concentrated in northwest Pakistan in areas along the Afghan border, where the group has used <a href="https://duranddispatch.com/strategic-messaging-september-2026-vol-2-issue-3/">tactics including</a> deadly suicide bombings, vehicle-borne improvised explosives and rockets. </p>

<p>Prior to the Kohat attack, IMP members were responsible for a May 2026 <a href="https://x.com/JawadYousufxai/status/2053307729457148192">checkpost assault</a> that killed 15 police and a July vehicle bomb attack at a <a href="https://www.dawn.com/news/2015898?">police station</a> in the city of Bannu. </p>

<p>The IMP styles itself as a unified front that brings various jihadist factions operating in Pakistan together under one command. Its recent propaganda, for example, includes a video by a religious cleric urging unity among jihadists. </p>

<p>That message aligns with that of <a href="https://www.rferl.org/a/how-a-resurgent-al-qaeda-is-helping-militant-attacks-in-pakistan/33846276.html">Al‑Qaida in the Indian Subcontinent, or AQIS</a>, to which the IMP is linked. In recent years, AQIS has sought to become the <a href="https://docs.un.org/en/S/2026/651">backbone of a united coalition</a> operating in the Afghanistan-Pakistan region.</p>

<p>But attempts to unify the various militant groups operating in Pakistan appear to have been undermined by the specifics of the Kohat attack.</p>

<p>Indeed, the targeting of a mosque – and the extent of civilian deaths – prompted an intra-jihadist quarrel. Within hours, the Pakistani Taliban and another group, Jamaat-ul-Ahrar, released statements <a href="https://www.memri.org/jttm/al-qaeda-indian-subcontinent-aqis-condemns-attack-pakistani-mosque-disavowed-two-tehrik-e">denouncing the attack</a> and disavowing any role. </p>

<p>The Afghan Taliban, whose leadership the Pakistani Taliban pledges allegiance to and which Islamabad accuses of sheltering the group, also <a href="https://thekabultribune.com/en/0011238">condemned the attack</a>. AQIS likewise criticized the attack and urged followers to avoid activities that could taint their aim, ideology and operations.</p>

<p>For AQIS, the fallout is particularly damaging: It had spent the preceding months showcasing IMP as a model affiliate and a unifying force in the contemporary jihadist landscape.</p>

<p>By mid-2026, AQIS was promoting the IMP as one of its <a href="https://thesoufancenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/25-Years-After-911-The-Future-Of-The-Global-Jihadi-Movement.pdf">global fronts</a>. The June–July issue of its flagship magazine, Nawa-e-Ghazwa-e-Hind, featured the IMP’s campaign in Pakistan in an infographic. And a May editorial had urged greater coordination among jihadi groups, citing IMP-aligned cooperation as the model.</p>

<h2>Militant convergence and competition</h2>

<p>The ongoing intra-group disquiet should not distract from the larger picture of violent extremism in the region. Pakistan is facing its most serious security crisis in two decades; the country now ranks first in the <a href="https://www.visionofhumanity.org/countries-most-impacted-by-terrorism-in-2026/">Global Terrorism Index</a>. </p>

<p>Driving this trend is a combination of organizational convergence and competition among extremist groups, including local and transnational jihadist groups, as well as <a href="https://theconversation.com/baloch-insurgency-suicide-bombs-and-uptick-in-violence-threaten-pakistan-regional-security-282513">separatist groups in the southwestern province of Balochistan</a>. </p>

<p>With respect to the jihadist groups, the <a href="https://thediplomat.com/2025/12/pakistans-worsening-threat-landscape-in-2025/">Pakistani Taliban has absorbed</a> more than a hundred factions since 2020, while AQIS has drawn the IMP into its orbit. </p>

<p>AQIS and the Pakistani Taliban, however, remain distinct entities. Though there have been indications of <a href="https://blog.prif.org/2025/01/21/the-resurgence-of-the-pakistani-taliban-implications-for-afghanistan-pakistan-relations/">occasional collaboration</a> in their activities, various attempts at a formal merger have repeatedly failed since 2020, owing to ideological differences that persist. Most notably, AQIS has transnational ambitions, while the Pakistani Taliban’s focus is on Pakistan.</p>

<p>This dynamic of convergence is also evident in Balochistan, where key ethnonationalist groups have consolidated since 2018 under the <a href="https://ctc.westpoint.edu/the-baloch-insurgency-in-pakistan-evolution-tactics-and-regional-security-implications/">Baloch Raaji Aajoi Sangar</a> umbrella.</p>

<p>At the same time, fault lines in the wider regional militant landscape have also driven violence. The <a href="https://www.csis.org/blogs/examining-extremism/examining-extremism-islamic-state-khorasan-province-iskp">Islamic State Khorasan Province</a> – the Islamic State group’s official affiliate in the region –  remains hostile to the Pakistani Taliban, AQIS and IMP alike – as well as to the Afghan Taliban and the Pakistani government. </p>

<p>As a transnational group competing with locally rooted actors, the Islamic State Khorasan Province, or ISKP, encourages a cascading trend of extreme violence.</p>

<p>A second subtler form of competition runs within the Pakistan Taliban-AQIS-IMP axis itself. Nominally allies, the groups compete for relevance, resources and recruits by outbidding one another with more extreme tactics. It is precisely that logic that appears to lie behind the Kohat attack.</p>

<h2>Cross-border tension</h2>

<p>Both the collusion and competition dynamics among groups are sustained by <a href="https://thesoufancenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/25-Years-After-911-The-Future-Of-The-Global-Jihadi-Movement.pdf">interstate tensions</a> that give militants the opportunity to exploit counterterrorism gaps. In particular, the <a href="https://warontherocks.com/open-war-at-the-durand-line-can-pakistans-escalation-compel-a-taliban-recalculation/">worsening relationship between Pakistan and Afghanistan</a> has entrenched many of the militant groups Pakistan is confronting.</p>

<p>Relations between the two countries have deteriorated since the Taliban seized control of Afghanistan in 2021. While Pakistan <a href="https://warontherocks.com/decoding-pakistans-2024-airstrikes-in-afghanistan/">began with tactics</a>  such as border closures, trade restrictions and limited strikes on Pakistan Taliban camps, intended to pressure the ruling Taliban to act against anti-Pakistan militants within its borders, it crossed into <a href="https://warontherocks.com/open-war-at-the-durand-line-can-pakistans-escalation-compel-a-taliban-recalculation/">open war</a> in February 2026. That’s when Pakistan struck Taliban military installations across the border in Afghanistan.</p>

<p>A <a href="https://duranddispatch.com/open-war-stalled-peace-cce1/">fragile ceasefire</a> followed, but it has been strained by continued <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/4/27/ceasefire-at-risk-as-pakistan-and-afghanistan-report-cross-border-attacks">cross-border attacks</a>, Pakistani <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jun/29/pakistan-deadly-airstrikes-afghanistan-border">airstrikes</a> on militant hideouts in Afghanistan, and <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/afghan-forces-struck-militant-hideouts-pakistan-taliban-says-2026-06-19/">Afghan Taliban strikes</a> on alleged ISKP bases in Pakistan.</p>

<p>For the Pakistani government, the Pakistani Taliban is an Afghan-based threat that the government in Kabul must act on. While for the ruling Taliban in Afghanistan, the Pakistani Taliban are a domestic issue for Pakistan to deal with.</p>

            </figcaption>

<p>Tensions were already escalating by the time the Kohat attack took place on Sept. 18. And the attack itself carried the two features most likely to inflame them.  </p>

<p>The group that claimed the attack is built around networks believed to <a href="https://jamestown.org/rise-and-growing-threat-of-ittehad-ul-mujahideen-pakistan/">operate from sanctuaries</a> across the border in Afghanistan; Pakistani authorities identified at least one of the bombers as an Afghan national. </p>

<p>For Islamabad, that was confirmation of the Afghan government’s complicity in the worsening security situation in Pakistan. The accusation carries a particular irony, since for decades, Pakistan’s military and intelligence establishment <a href="https://www.cfr.org/articles/pakistans-support-taliban-what-know">nurtured the Afghan Taliban</a> as a strategic asset. When the Taliban retook Kabul in August 2021, <a href="https://www.geo.tv/latest/365546-afghanistan-has-broken-shackles-of-slavery-pm-imran-khan">Pakistani leaders celebrated</a>, expecting it to <a href="https://southasianvoices.org/the-untenable-ttp-pakistan-negotiations/">rein in</a> the Pakistani Taliban. The Afghan Taliban, on the other hand, has been willing to <a href="https://southasianvoices.org/the-untenable-ttp-pakistan-negotiations/">facilitate talks</a> between Islamabad and the Pakistani Taliban, but not to crack down on a group that it <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/17467586.2023.2280924">fought alongside</a> against U.S.-led forces for well over a decade.</p>

<p>As such, the Kohat attack has hardened, rather than merely reinforced, Pakistan’s demand that Kabul dismantle militant sanctuaries. The retaliatory strikes that have followed – Pakistan’s first airstrikes on Afghan soil since June – have merely reopened the cycle of Pakistani cross-border action and Afghan retaliation.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292416/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Trump speculates on diesel fuel export ban as high prices ripple across US economy</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761278/original/file-20260921-50-61ahv3.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=3%2C0%2C6662%2C4439&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Demand for rail freight shipping is up, as trucking becomes more expensive. Both use diesel fuel, but trains are more efficient at carrying heavy loads long distances.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/freight-is-transferred-between-rail-and-trucks-at-the-bnsf-news-photo/2295807697">Scott Olson/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Diesel fuel powers long-distance trucks, freight locomotives, boats and barges, farm machinery, construction and mining equipment, and backup generators. Its concentrated energy <a href="https://www.coherentmarketinsights.com/industry-reports/diesel-engines-market">powers efficient engines that can haul heavy loads and refuel machines quickly</a>. Those are all excellent attributes for long periods of heavy work on the move or in locations not connected to the electricity grid.</p>

<p>So when diesel prices hit record highs, as they have, that increases the costs of essentials like food, transportation and even other energy sources. On Sept. 14, 2026, the U.S. Energy Information Administration said <a href="https://www.eia.gov/petroleum/gasdiesel">national average diesel prices were US$6.52 a gallon</a>, which is up more than 23 cents – 3.6% – from a week earlier, and up nearly $2.78 – 74% – since the same week in 2025.</p>

<p>The U.S. war with Iran, and to a lesser extent the Russian war with Ukraine, have <a href="https://theconversation.com/iran-war-pushes-diesel-the-economys-lifeblood-to-record-high-prices-with-no-relief-on-the-horizon-292049">disrupted oil production, refinery output and petroleum supply chains</a> across the world, which are part of <a href="https://biocomplexity.virginia.edu/our-team/vidya-mani">my field of study</a> on how geopolitical friction reshapes global supply chains. These conflicts have gone on long enough now – more than six months between the <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/six-consequences-six-months-war-iran-2026-08-27/">U.S. and Iran</a>, and more than a four years of direct battle between <a href="https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/02/1167019">Russia and Ukraine</a> – that most companies and countries have run out of any extra supplies they might have had <a href="https://www.iea.org/topics/the-middle-east-and-global-energy-markets">on hand</a>.</p>

<p>The <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-shadow-tankers-are-the-only-ships-still-moving-through-the-strait-of-hormuz-277785">near-complete closure</a> of the Strait of Hormuz has <a href="https://www.iea.org/reports/oil-market-report-september-2026">dramatically reduced the flow of crude oil</a> across the world – a raw material necessary for producing gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and heating oil. Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, which have <a href="https://www.iea.org/commentaries/russian-refining-sector-struggles-amid-intensifying-ukrainian-attacks">intensified through 2026</a>, have restricted the flow of Russian diesel to the <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/russia-set-extend-diesel-export-ban-until-end-october-vedomosti-reports-2026-09-16/">global market</a>.</p>

<p>Put together, all this means that there’s not much diesel fuel left lying around, and lots of people want to buy what is available, as well as what little is produced each day. It’s all a matter of supply and demand. If demand remains constant and supply drops, prices rise. The effects of rising prices are broad and widespread both economically and geographically. </p>

<h2>Food and retail</h2>

<p>Farming and harvesting are seasonal operations that depend heavily on diesel-powered equipment. When farmers face high fuel costs, they may <a href="https://apnews.com/article/diesel-prices-record-farmers-harvest-c320c9811a74654888255a4b4aff3d06">restrict or postpone their planting and harvesting operations</a>, which means less food is produced for sale to markets and customers.</p>

<p>Higher diesel costs also translate into <a href="https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/high-us-diesel-prices-put-052953417.html">higher processing and transportation costs</a> for food and basic staples. In particular, refrigerated trucks carrying vegetables, dairy and meat products to retail markets are <a href="https://time.com/article/2026/09/11/us-diesel-prices-record-high-impact-groceries-american-consumers/">heavily dependent on diesel</a>.</p>



<h2>Truck freight</h2>

<p>Long-haul trucks move consumer goods across the country from warehouses and distribution centers to retail stores and homes. A trucking industry research firm has estimated that a 20% increase in fuel costs can translate into a <a href="https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/new-atri-report-details-accelerating-costs-and-low-profitability-despite-cuts-302826514.html">4% increase in operating costs</a>.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.wbng.com/2026/09/16/diesel-prices-hit-record-high-straining-new-york-trucking-industry/">Trucking is not a high-profit-margin business</a>. So any increase in costs gets passed on to the consumers who buy whatever is being shipped.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761282/original/file-20260921-50-m1mmkd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A tractor tows fertilizing equipment across a field." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761282/original/file-20260921-50-m1mmkd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761282/original/file-20260921-50-m1mmkd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761282/original/file-20260921-50-m1mmkd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761282/original/file-20260921-50-m1mmkd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761282/original/file-20260921-50-m1mmkd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761282/original/file-20260921-50-m1mmkd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761282/original/file-20260921-50-m1mmkd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
