              <span class="caption">Many pieces of farm equipment and machinery use diesel fuel to produce food.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/grass-lake-michigan-a-farmer-applies-liquid-fertilizer-to-a-news-photo/2275015674">Jim West/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Public transit</h2>

<p>High diesel prices have a double effect on public transit. </p>

<p>First, buses and trains powered by diesel fuel incur a direct increase in fuel costs.</p>

<p>Second, the crude oil supply shortages have led to higher <a href="https://www.wsj.com/business/energy-oil/americans-have-spent-100-billion-more-on-fuel-during-the-iran-war-377952a1">diesel and gasoline prices</a>. When gas is expensive, people shift to public transit to <a href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/5-gas-pushing-americans-cars-173038652.html">save money</a>, leading to increased demand for transit. </p>

<p>Although diesel prices have spiked faster and stayed higher longer than <a href="https://www.jpmorgan.com/insights/markets-and-economy/economy/diesel-prices-hit-new-record-september-2026-what-it-means-for-inflation-and-investors">prices for gasoline</a>, passengers save money by sharing the costs of transit.</p>

<p>Air fares also more expensive, because <a href="https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/travel/our-insights/what-could-rising-fuel-costs-mean-for-airlines">diesel and jet fuel are produced from the same production process</a>.</p>

<h2>Energy systems</h2>

<p>Diesel is used for a <a href="https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=427&amp;t=3">relatively small percentage</a> of U.S. power generation, but it’s <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.erss.2025.104124">substantially more common in many countries</a>, including where there aren’t widespread interconnected power grids. Anyone using diesel generators for primary or backup power has to pay more for diesel.</p>

<p>And shortages of crude oil supplies and loss of refinery production capacity means less availability of less heating oil – which is also produced through the same process as diesel. That is expected to lead to <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/heating-oil-bills-winter-iran-war/">higher energy prices for consumers in the coming winter</a>. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761283/original/file-20260921-70-8kpioj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="An aerial view shows an industrial site with tanks and pipes and smokestacks." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761283/original/file-20260921-70-8kpioj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761283/original/file-20260921-70-8kpioj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=449&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761283/original/file-20260921-70-8kpioj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=449&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761283/original/file-20260921-70-8kpioj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=449&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761283/original/file-20260921-70-8kpioj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=565&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761283/original/file-20260921-70-8kpioj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=565&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761283/original/file-20260921-70-8kpioj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=565&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>

<h2>Consumer prices</h2>

<p>Consumers will experience different price changes depending on their locations, which affects both the distances goods need to travel and the amounts of fuel available.</p>

<p>For instance, the average diesel price in California has topped <a href="https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/california-diesel-tops-8-gallon-163053549.html">$8 per gallon</a>, but the <a href="https://smallfleethq.com/fuel-cards/diesel/gulf-coast">Gulf Coast</a> is seeing a relatively cheaper price of $6.03 a gallon. </p>

<p>In part, that difference is because there are many refineries and terminals along the <a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=7170">Gulf Coast</a>, while <a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=65184">California has very few pipeline connections</a> to other refining regions. Its refineries depend on crude oil imports from the <a href="https://www.wsj.com/business/energy-oil/the-iran-war-is-hitting-california-harder-than-any-other-state-24bb289e">Middle East</a>.</p>

<p>In addition, California’s efforts to curb air pollution mean it <a href="https://ww2.arb.ca.gov/our-work/programs/diesel-fuel">requires a more refined version of diesel fuel that emits fewer pollutants</a>. So fuel companies in California can’t just bring in diesel from elsewhere.</p>

<p><a href="https://theconversation.com/suspending-federal-gas-tax-wouldnt-save-drivers-as-much-as-they-might-hope-heres-what-goes-into-the-price-of-a-gallon-of-gas-282702">Taxes and fuel surcharges</a> also make a difference in diesel prices. The federal government imposes a <a href="https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=10&amp;t=10">flat tax on diesel of 24.4 cents a gallon</a>. But state and local taxes vary. California’s <a href="https://cdtfa.ca.gov/taxes-and-fees/sales-tax-rates-for-fuels.htm">state diesel tax is 48.2 cents a gallon</a>, plus a 13% sales-tax rate, on top of which there may be additional local taxes. </p>

<p>In some cases, state policies to lower these taxes are thwarted. In Georgia, where <a href="https://www.multistate.us/insider/2026/4/6/lawmakers-push-fuel-tax-relief-amid-rising-gas-costs">state lawmakers suspended fuel taxes</a> from March through June 2026, many counties kept their taxes on fuel sales.</p>

<h2>A diesel export ban?</h2>

<p>In part to fuel its own military’s efforts in Ukraine, but also to help keep its domestic economy going, Russia – normally the <a href="https://universaltrades.co/blog/top-10-diesel-exporting-countries-en/">world’s second-largest diesel exporter</a> after the U.S. – <a href="https://www.spglobal.com/energy/en/news-research/latest-news/crude-oil/072726-russia-extends-gasoline-export-ban-until-end-of-2026">suspended diesel exports in early July 2026</a>, and has extended that until at least the end of the year.</p>

<p>The customers whose demand was formerly met by Russian diesel are now seeking other sources. Diesel producers in the U.S. are raising their prices at home, because they could <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/us-fuel-exports-hit-record-march-asia-europe-sought-replace-middle-east-supplies-2026-04-01/">make more money selling their fuel overseas</a>.</p>

<p>The U.S. actually produces <a href="https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/diesel-fuel/use-of-diesel.php">more diesel fuel than it consumes</a>. But it still imports some, because it’s not always easy to get U.S. diesel from where it’s produced to where it’s used. Sometimes, and some places, it’s easier to ship in diesel from elsewhere. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761285/original/file-20260921-50-fumuyp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A sign outside a gas station says 'we have diesel.'" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761285/original/file-20260921-50-fumuyp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761285/original/file-20260921-50-fumuyp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761285/original/file-20260921-50-fumuyp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761285/original/file-20260921-50-fumuyp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761285/original/file-20260921-50-fumuyp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761285/original/file-20260921-50-fumuyp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761285/original/file-20260921-50-fumuyp.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Not all gas stations have diesel fuel – the ones that do are making it known.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/sign-advertises-diesel-fuel-at-a-brooklyn-gas-station-on-news-photo/2273576625">Spencer Platt/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Some Republicans in Congress have <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/senate/6102916-senate-gop-diesel-export-ban/">proposed a ban on diesel exports</a> from the U.S., and <a href="https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-09-22/trump-says-he-s-pushed-for-fuel-export-ban-amid-price-crunch">President Donald Trump has said he supports one</a>. If that were to happen, it could help make diesel cheaper, especially near Gulf Coast refineries that normally export a lot of their diesel. It could put less upward pressure on trucking and equipment bills and consumer prices. </p>

<p>But the benefits would depend on how long the ban lasted, what exactly it banned, how diesel was moved around the U.S. and how much of their savings oil companies, trucking companies and merchants passed on to regular Americans.</p>

<p>There are substantial risks, too. Without export shipping to handle the volume, fuel storage near refineries may fill up. If it can’t be moved easily and economically to other states, refineries could reduce how much diesel they make – which would mean also cutting production of gasoline, jet fuel and heating oil.</p>

<p>And overseas diesel prices would likely rise if U.S. exports disappeared, meaning regions in the U.S. that still need imports would pay even more, not less. A diesel-export ban could offer short-term relief to some buyers while shifting costs to others or weakening production incentives.</p>

<p>The energy crunch from the two wars and continued attacks on production and transportation infrastructure will continue to affect the U.S. and global economy for an extended period. Alternate shipping routes, release of reserves, export bans and additional subsidies are some of the short-term measures that can alleviate the worst of the pain. </p>

<p>But until crude oil production and refinery capacity expands, people will need to live with higher prices.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292323/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>¿Por qué los hispanos en Estados Unidos están perdiendo la fe en el sueño americano?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760356/original/file-20260915-50-y9df1w.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C215%2C7269%2C4845&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Un desfile del Día de la Independencia en Los Ángeles, que se canceló en 2025 debido a las redadas del ICE, volvió a celebrarse en 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/participants-wear-american-flags-while-marching-in-the-67th-news-photo/2283627185">Mario Tama/Getty Images News via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Donald Trump obtuvo <a href="https://apnews.com/projects/election-results-2024/votecast/">el 43% del voto hispano en 2024</a>, frente al <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trumps-favorability-has-fallen-among-hispanics-since-january-a-new-ap-norc-poll-finds">35% en 2020</a>, un avance importante para los republicanos. Ahora, a medida que se acercan las elecciones de mitad de mandato, los hispanos en Estados Unidos, independientemente de su afiliación política, están perdiendo la fe en el sueño americano, y las actuales políticas migratorias podrían explicar en parte esta tendencia.</p>

<p>Los arrestos <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2026/08/27/us/ice-immigrant-arrests-trump-deportation-dhs.html">de personas sin antecedentes penales</a> realizados por el Servicio de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE, por sus siglas en inglés) están aumentando. Desde el año pasado, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/08/us/immigration-agent-shootings-vehicles.html">agentes federales de inmigración han disparado</a> contra casi dos docenas de personas — la mayoría de ellas latinas— según The New York Times. Entre ellas figuran <a href="https://www.houstonchronicle.com/news/houston-texas/trending/article/montrose-salgado-protest-22349402.php">Lorenzo Salgado Araujo</a> y <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/07/13/us/live-news/maine-ice-shooting-houston-minnesota">Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero,</a> quienes fallecieron en Texas y Maine, respectivamente.</p>

<p>Este clima de mayor control migratorio puede estar afectando el sentido de pertenencia de los hispanos y su creencia de que pueden aspirar a una vida mejor en Estados Unidos. La encuesta de 2026 del Public Religion Research Institute (PRRI) <a href="https://prri.org/research/competing-visions-of-america-politics-religion-and-american-identity/">sobre la identidad estadounidense</a> preguntó a más de 5.000 adultos qué pensaban sobre el sueño americano: la idea de que, si uno trabaja duro, puede salir adelante. Solo el 40% de los hispanos en Estados Unidos afirma que <a href="https://prri.org/research/competing-visions-of-america-politics-religion-and-american-identity/">ese sueño sigue siendo una realidad hoy en día</a>, frente al 52% hace apenas dos años.</p>

<p>Soy <a href="https://prri.org/staff/diana-orces-ph-d/">directora de investigación de PRRI</a> y estudio la opinión pública y la inmigración. Recientemente analicé casi 700 respuestas de hispanoamericanos a esta encuesta para entender qué factores están asociados con la creencia de que el sueño americano ya no es una realidad. Encontré que el orgullo nacional, la preocupación por los derechos y las libertades democráticas, el apego a Estados Unidos y las opiniones sobre el manejo de la inmigración por parte de la administración de Trump están significativamente asociados con esta creencia.</p>

<p>Sorprendentemente, la afiliación política no lo está.</p>

<p>Entre los hispanos en Estados Unidos – republicanos, demócratas e independientes— está creciendo una sensación de aislamiento al sentirse menos seguros, menos bienvenidos y cada vez más como extraños en su propio país.</p>

<h2>Cambios de opinión</h2>

<p>El porcentaje de hispanos en Estados Unidos que se identifican como republicanos <a href="https://prri.org/spotlight/exploring-the-diverse-religious-and-political-affiliations-of-hispanic-americans/">se ha duplicado</a>, pasando del 10% en 2013 al 21% en 2025. Sin embargo, durante el último año, <a href="https://prri.org/research/competing-visions-of-america-politics-religion-and-american-identity/">la opinión favorable de los hispanos sobre el manejo de la inmigración</a> por parte de la administración de Trump han disminuido, del <a href="https://prri.org/research/democracy-at-a-crossroads-how-americans-view-trumps-first-100-days-in-office/">31% en 2025</a> al 19% en 2026.</p>

<p>La posibilidad de que los republicanos mantengan sus recientes ganancias electorales entre los votantes hispanos en las elecciones de mitad de mandato de noviembre de 2026 dependerá de si estos consideran que la administración ha hecho que sus familias se sientan menos seguras y que su situación económica sea más incierta. La mayoría de los hispanoamericanos — el 68% — cree que <a href="https://prri.org/research/americans-views-on-immigration-enforcement-ice-and-civil-liberties-in-the-second-trump-administration/">el aumento de agentes de ICE</a> está haciendo que las comunidades sean menos seguras.</p>

<p>El orgullo nacional también ha disminuido. Solo el 42% de los hispanoamericanos afirma sentirse <a href="https://prri.org/research/competing-visions-of-america-politics-religion-and-american-identity/">extremadamente o muy orgulloso de ser estadounidense</a>, frente al 51% de los estadounidenses en general. Sin duda, el orgullo nacional ha disminuido considerablemente en todo el país, pasando del <a href="https://prri.org/research/july-2013-prri-rns/">82% en 2013</a> al 51% en la actualidad. Pero entre los hispanoamericanos, este declive ha sido aún más pronunciado: <a href="https://prri.org/research/competing-visions-of-america-politics-religion-and-american-identity/">del 77% al 42%</a>. La mayoría de los hispanoamericanos — el 56% — afirma ahora <a href="https://prri.org/research/trumps-unprecedented-actions-deepen-asymmetric-divides/">sentirse como extraños en su propio país</a>.</p>

<p>La preocupación sobre el estado de la democracia también puede estar contribuyendo a estos cambios de opinión. Cuando los ciudadanos con derecho al voto temen ser privados de este derecho debido a <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/16/us/politics/trump-again-makes-unfounded-claims-of-noncitizen-voting.html">la difusión de información no fundamentada</a> sobre el voto de personas que no son ciudadanas, ese temor puede debilitar tanto su sentido de pertenencia como su confianza en las instituciones democráticas.</p>

<p>Investigaciones pasadas muestran que los <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0731121420966620">ciudadanos latinos ya se ven afectados de manera desproporcionada por las estrictas políticas de identificación de votantes</a>. Los investigadores sugieren que esto puede deberse en parte <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1532673X18810012">a que tienen menos probabilidades de contar con una identificación</a> y a que pueden sentirse intimidados por un entorno migratorio cada vez más hostil, que podría poner en riesgo a sus familiares indocumentados. La propuesta de ley <a href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/7296">SAVE America Act</a>, que <a href="https://theconversation.com/republicans-control-congress-so-why-is-trumps-save-america-act-stuck-287156">exigiría documentación adicional para votar</a>, dificultaría aún más su participación electoral.</p>

<h2>Pérdida de fe en el sueño americano</h2>

<p>Para entender mejor qué piensan los hispanos en Estados Unidos sobre el sueño americano, analicé <a href="https://prri.org/research/competing-visions-of-america-politics-religion-and-american-identity/">la encuesta de PRRI</a>, teniendo en cuenta diferencias de raza, edad, género, educación, religión, situación laboral, ingresos, región, ser padre o madre, idioma de la encuesta y afiliación política. Incluso después de tomar en cuenta estos factores, las opiniones desfavorables sobre el actual manejo de la inmigración continuaron siendo estadísticamente significativas. Menores niveles de orgullo nacional, un menor apego a Estados Unidos y la preocupación por los derechos democráticos también están significativamente asociados con la creencia de que el sueño americano ya no es una realidad.</p>

<p>Otro factor resultó estadísticamente significativo: el idioma de la encuesta.</p>

<p>Contrario a lo esperado, los hispanos que respondieron la encuesta en español fueron más propensos a creer que el sueño americano continúa siendo una realidad que quienes la respondieron en inglés. Esto podría deberse a que algunos de los encuestados en español evalúan las oportunidades económicas en Estados Unidos en comparación con las de sus países de origen.</p>

<p>Un factor que no resultó estadísticamente significativo fue la afiliación política.</p>

<p>Después de tomar en cuenta otras características, no existen diferencias estadísticamente significativas entre hispanos demócratas, republicanos e independientes en cuanto a su creencia sobre el sueño americano. Esto sugiere que la pérdida de fe va más allá de su afiliación política y puede reflejar preocupaciones más profundas sobre su sentido de pertenencia.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/US/RHI725225">En Estados Unidos, una de cada cinco personas</a> se identifica como hispana. Cuando un segmento cada vez mayor de la sociedad estadounidense empieza a dudar de que el trabajo duro brinda mejores oportunidades, de que la ciudadanía proporciona mayor seguridad o de que la participación conduce a una mayor aceptación, las consecuencias van más allá de qué partido apoyarán en noviembre. La pregunta más de fondo es si las personas están comenzando a perder la fe no solo en su propio país, sino también en sus promesas democráticas y en el futuro que este les ofrece.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292206/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Fiber is both diet fad and fixture for good health – a doctor explains why there is no one-size-fits-all way to increase your intake</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759964/original/file-20260915-50-idxor6.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=180%2C0%2C1948%2C1298&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Many whole foods, such as fruits, vegetables, legumes and nuts, are high in fiber.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/high-fiber-foods-royalty-free-image/1020930592">bit245/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>The numbers are clear: <a href="https://nutrition.org/most-americans-are-not-getting-enough-fiber-in-our-diets/">Americans aren’t getting enough fiber</a>. </p>

<p>Research has consistently shown that high-fiber diets are linked to <a href="https://theconversation.com/fiber-is-your-bodys-natural-guide-to-weight-management-rather-than-cutting-carbs-out-of-your-diet-eat-them-in-their-original-fiber-packaging-instead-205159">significant health benefits</a>, including a lower risk of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2020-054370">cardiovascular disease and colorectal cancer</a>, as well as <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s13075-023-03126-3">improved arthritis symptoms</a>. </p>

<p>Despite these benefits, there remains a <a href="https://doi.org/10.3945/jn.112.160176">significant fiber gap</a> in the typical American diet. The recommended daily fiber intake is 25 grams a day for women and 38 grams a day for men. From 2013 to 2018, only <a href="http://doi.org/10.1017/S0007114523000089">4% of U.S. adults met their recommended adequate intake</a> for dietary fiber. The average fiber intake was about 16 grams a day.</p>

<p>Adding fiber to your diet through eating more fiber-rich foods or by taking fiber supplements has become a <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/05/18/nx-s1-5821598/fibermaxxing-healthy-fiber-foods-diet-benefits">viral health trend</a>. At the same time, the 2025 update to the American dietary guidelines <a href="https://cdn.realfood.gov/DGA.pdf">appears to downplay fiber’s role</a> in a healthy diet, placing high-fiber whole grains at the bottom as the smallest part of the inverted food pyramid. This can be confusing, because the written guidelines themselves continue to highlight the importance of eating whole grains.</p>

<p>What does the science say about the health benefits of a high-fiber diet? And what steps can you take to incorporate more fiber into your diet? These and similar questions my patients have asked me <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=8xTeCo0AAAAJ&amp;hl=en">as a physician-scientist</a> prompted me to look further into the latest research on dietary fiber.</p>

<h2>Basics of dietary fiber</h2>

<p>Dietary fiber can be found in many sources, and the choices can be overwhelming.</p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/advances/nmab116">Dietary fiber</a> refers to carbohydrates your body can’t digest. Many <a href="https://www.mayoclinic.org/healthy-lifestyle/nutrition-and-healthy-eating/in-depth/high-fiber-foods/art-20050948">whole foods are high in fiber</a>. High-fiber foods include raspberries, avocados, oats and other whole grains, and lentils and other legumes.</p>

<p>Fiber also comes in supplements such as <a href="https://doi.org/10.1039/d2fo00560c">psyllium husk powder</a>, known as the brand Metamucil, which comes from a plant called <em>Plantago ovata</em>. Isolated fibers <a href="https://doi.org/10.1039/d2fo01096h">such as inulin</a> are now increasingly added to foods, including those marketed as high-fiber snack bars, keto-friendly carbs and even soda.</p>

<p>Moreover, not all <a href="https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2020-054370">types of fiber</a> are created equal. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759770/original/file-20260914-50-7yt3ot.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Flow chart of various types of fiber, including soluble, viscous fermentable fibre; soluble, viscous, non-fermentable fibre; soluble, non-viscous, fermentable fibre; soluble, non-viscous, fermentable fibre; insoluble, partially" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759770/original/file-20260914-50-7yt3ot.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759770/original/file-20260914-50-7yt3ot.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=382&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759770/original/file-20260914-50-7yt3ot.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=382&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759770/original/file-20260914-50-7yt3ot.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=382&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759770/original/file-20260914-50-7yt3ot.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=480&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759770/original/file-20260914-50-7yt3ot.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=480&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759770/original/file-20260914-50-7yt3ot.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=480&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">There are many types of fiber, each with different health benefits.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2020-054370">McKeown et al./BMJ</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/">CC BY-NC</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>For example, psyllium is a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jand.2016.09.021">viscous fiber</a>, meaning it forms a gel when added to water. This gel can contribute to early satiety, meaning you feel fuller after eating. Viscous fiber can help lower cholesterol, improve blood sugar levels and blood pressure, lead to a small amount of weight loss, and make bowel movements more regular.</p>

<p>Other popular types of <a href="https://theconversation.com/gut-microbes-are-the-community-within-you-that-you-cant-live-without-how-eating-well-can-cultivate-your-microbial-and-social-self-210668">fiber are fermented</a>, meaning they are eaten and processed by bacteria that live in your gut. These gut bacteria make proteins that can lower inflammation in the body. Inulin is one type of fermented fiber and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.indcrop.2021.113726">can be extracted</a> from chicory root and Jerusalem artichokes.</p>

<p>Nutrition experts recommend getting a variety of fiber-rich foods in your diet because of the added benefit of other nutrients in these foods, such as <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/ajcn/78.3.579S">antioxidants</a>. </p>

<h2>Probiotics versus fiber</h2>

<p>Besides fiber, adding <a href="https://theconversation.com/bacteria-in-your-gut-can-improve-your-mood-new-research-in-mice-tries-to-zero-in-on-the-crucial-strains-220935">probiotics</a> to your diet may also benefit your gut health.</p>

<p>Probiotics are a category of fermented foods that still contain live microbes when you eat them. These include <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41575-020-00390-5">fermented foods</a> such as sauerkraut, yogurt and kimchi, which are changed by the addition of live microbes, such as bacteria or yeast. Although the terms sound similar, these fermented foods that have “good” bacteria added to them are not the same as the fiber that gets fermented by bacteria already in your gut.</p>

<p>Think of it this way: Fiber provides the material for the gut bacteria to work with. Probiotics provide more “good” gut bacteria to join the community that already exists.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759967/original/file-20260915-50-6j81qe.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Close-up of a person filling a jar with homemade kimchi" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759967/original/file-20260915-50-6j81qe.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/759967/original/file-20260915-50-6j81qe.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759967/original/file-20260915-50-6j81qe.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759967/original/file-20260915-50-6j81qe.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759967/original/file-20260915-50-6j81qe.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759967/original/file-20260915-50-6j81qe.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/759967/original/file-20260915-50-6j81qe.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In a 2021 study, researchers <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2021.06.019">examined the gut microbiomes</a> of 36 healthy adults who either ate a diet high in fiber or a diet high in fermented foods. They found that those who ate a high-fiber diet had a <a href="https://theconversation.com/hangry-bacteria-in-your-gut-microbiome-are-linked-to-chronic-disease-feeding-them-what-they-need-could-lead-to-happier-cells-and-a-healthier-body-199486">gut microbiome</a> that was more active in making the enzymes that break down fiber. That means these microbes got better at using the fiber they were fed to make byproducts helpful for the body.</p>

<p>In contrast, those who ate a diet high in fermented foods had a gut microbiome that was more diverse, meaning they had many different species of bacteria in their guts. They also had lower levels of inflammation. Many chronic conditions can raise levels of inflammation in the body, and exposure to inflammation can put stress on the body, contributing to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2025.08.047">issues such as cardiovascular disease</a>. </p>

<p>The results of this small study point to the possibility that combining high-fiber and fermented foods in your diet could synergize their health benefits in nourishing the gut microbiome.</p>

<h2>How can you get more fiber in your diet?</h2>

<p>With so many options available, what’s the best way to increase your fiber intake?</p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/02601060251348552">Some barriers</a> to eating enough dietary fiber include cost, accessibility and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/advances/nmac091">tolerability</a>. Some high-fiber whole foods, such as berries, can be expensive. Highly fermentable fibers, such as inulin, often <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jada.2010.03.025">cause bloating and discomfort</a>, especially if you aren’t used to eating them. This can be a turnoff for high-fiber drinks and snacks, since they contain so much fiber in a single serving.</p>

<p>There are many ways to increase the amount of fiber you eat on a daily basis. The <a href="https://www.uclahealth.org/news/article/beat-bloat-4-tips-increasing-your-fiber-intake">general recommendation</a> is to do it slowly to allow your body to get used to the higher amount of fiber and to stay hydrated so your body can use the water along with the fiber for optimal bowel health. </p>

<p>Most importantly, try a variety of fiber sources to figure out what’s right for you. Some people will be able to reach the recommended fiber levels by eating whole foods alone; others will add supplements or eat foods with added fiber. There is no one-size-fits-all healthy diet. </p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Unlocking the full benefits of fiber</h2>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/advances/nmaa109">More focused research</a> is needed to understand more about the types of fiber that are beneficial to health, in what doses, and in what combinations. But these nutrition studies can be tricky. </p>

<p>My research focuses on finding links between fiber and different diseases in observational data and figuring out how to test them in a clinical trial. For example, one large observational study found an association between higher self-reported intake of whole grains and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1136/annrheumdis-2016-210810">lower risk of arthritis</a>. But researchers still need to test this connection in clinical trials, which requires deciding the right type and amount of whole grains to recommend, as well as the right length of time to test this diet.</p>

<p>While there have been many small clinical trials on fiber, they have not been big enough, specific enough or broad enough to provide answers that can be put into guidelines for everyone. Adequate funding has been one major hurdle to starting such large, well-designed trials. </p>

<p>At the same time, scientists already know many confirmed benefits of dietary fiber, and the gap lies in <a href="https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2020-054370">educating the public</a> and making changes so that foods high in fiber are affordable and accessible to more people.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/290023/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Dementia caregiving can expose hidden family tensions – but early planning can ease the strain</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760891/original/file-20260918-50-6ykwcd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=7%2C0%2C6114%2C4076&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Caring for someone with dementia can be especially challenging because the condition can profoundly change how a person interacts with their loved ones.  </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.agewithoutlimits.org/image-library/">Peter Kindersley via Centre for Ageing Better</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/">CC BY</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>“Families are messy, aren’t they?” a daughter commented during a series of focus groups I ran with <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/15333175251357328">caregivers of older adults with memory issues</a>. </p>

<p>Many people would agree with that sentiment. The <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jagp.2017.12.004">complexity can be compounded</a> when caring for someone who has a disease such as Alzheimer’s or another form of dementia that impairs their <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/14713012251324705">memory, language and sometimes personality</a>. </p>

<p>Yet discussing how caring for their loved one affects family dynamics – be it longstanding family feuds, unmet expectations about family responsibilities or the desire to keep health issues private – is often seen as taboo. </p>

<p>I am a sociologist and demographer <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=tFkt-zEAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">studying how family dynamics</a> change as people get older and need care – and how that relates to expectations about caregiving for older adults.</p>

<p>The makeup of families is changing, and that’s shaking up how caregiving can reverberate through family relationships. Caring for <a href="https://theconversation.com/family-and-friends-shoulder-the-real-cost-of-dementia-224b-in-unpaid-care-256782">family members or friends with dementia</a> can be especially thorny because of the ways the condition changes how a person behaves and how they <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jagp.2017.12.004">interact with others</a>. But a little planning and support can help families through the challenges. </p>

<h2>Caregiving is a common experience</h2>

<p>Americans are living much longer, which means that people are sharing <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s13524-019-00766-6">more years of their lives</a> with their family members. For instance, children are more likely to have <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s13524-019-00795-1">a living grandparent</a> today than in previous generations. </p>

<p>And that means it’s more likely that people will have a parent or grandparent who may experience cognitive decline at some point in their lives.</p>

<p>More than 5 million U.S. adults age 65 and older are currently <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/alz70860_101358">living with dementia</a> – an umbrella term describing a <a href="https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/alzheimers-and-dementia/what-dementia-symptoms-types-and-diagnosis">loss of cognitive abilities</a> around thinking, remembering and reasoning. That number is expected to reach over <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jalz.2018.06.3063">13 million by 2060</a> as the baby boomers age. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760896/original/file-20260918-71-oj8l2g.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Multigenerational family laughing together on sofa at home." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760896/original/file-20260918-71-oj8l2g.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760896/original/file-20260918-71-oj8l2g.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760896/original/file-20260918-71-oj8l2g.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760896/original/file-20260918-71-oj8l2g.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760896/original/file-20260918-71-oj8l2g.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760896/original/file-20260918-71-oj8l2g.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760896/original/file-20260918-71-oj8l2g.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Caregiving for people with dementia is a family affair.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/multigenerational-family-laughing-together-on-sofa-royalty-free-image/2264358194">Flashpop/DigitalVision via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>



<p>People with dementia interact with many people in their families and communities. Over half of Americans say that they <a href="https://ropercenter.cornell.edu/ipoll/search?q=USAP.071311.R20">know someone with dementia</a>, and more than a third of extended families <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/alz.70451">include an older adult with dementia</a>. In 2022, over 5 million family caregivers were <a href="https://doi.org/10.1377/hlthaff.2024.00978">taking care of an older adult with dementia</a>. That’s 1 out of every 5 people caring for an older adult in the U.S. </p>

<p>At the same time, family sizes are shrinking, and more <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/geronb/gbx068">older adults do not have children</a> or their children live far away – and more distance often <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.socscimed.2021.114627">equates to less caregiving</a>. Meanwhile, cultural acceptance of the idea of <a href="https://theconversation.com/the-real-reason-many-americans-are-cutting-ties-with-their-parents-and-siblings-283957">family estrangement</a> or going “no contact” has increased – as has a growing recognition of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/jomf.70065">chosen family</a>. That means more older adults are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0164027520907332">aging alone</a>, with limited support, or with other people who may not have the legal benefits of immediate family. </p>

<p>The caregiving landscape is shifting, too. </p>

<p>Historically, middle-age women were the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/geront/gnx093">largest group of caregivers</a> – generally, the daughters of aging parents. Adult children continue to be the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1377/hlthaff.2024.00978">largest group of caregivers</a> for older adults with dementia in the U.S., but their characteristics are changing. </p>

<p>Today, more caregivers are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1377/hlthaff.2024.00978">age 65 and older themselves</a>. And <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/jomf.70030">more men</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1215/00703370-11383976">young people</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.21697">friends are also providing care</a>. </p>

<p>All these factors combined are changing who is available to provide care for aging family members. </p>

<h2>Great expectations</h2>

<p>Dementia can amplify both expectations and family messiness. </p>

<p>Using data from a survey conducted by the RAND Corporation, a nonprofit research organization, my colleagues and I found that Americans feel <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/bsa3.70066">families have a greater responsibility</a> to care for an older relative with dementia than for a relative with a physical illness.</p>

<p>These expectations can <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/10748407241288606">motivate some caregivers</a> to provide care, even in difficult circumstances. But for others, old family disagreements, rivalries or unresolved points of tension can continue to haunt relationships in ways that can clash with <a href="https://nyupress.org/9781479813339/families-we-keep/">family expectations</a> around caretaking. </p>

<p>Dementia further complicates these feelings. For instance, one participant in our focus groups described a friend who struggled with caregiving because he felt compelled to do it even though his dad had not cared for him when he was a child. </p>

<p>Shrinking families also leads to constrained options. Some caregivers report feeling <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s12529-023-10246-2">they have no choice</a> but to provide care, especially when the older adult has dementia. In our focus groups, this was often because no one else was available due to small family sizes or even family estrangement. </p>

<p>Caring for someone with dementia often requires a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/geronb/gbz065">large circle of support</a>, leading to potential <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/geront/gnag040">clashes between family members</a>. In our focus groups, this played out as caregivers disagreeing on roles and responsibilities in ways that often reflected prior family tensions. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/i41c4246n8k?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Changing family structures are shaking up who’s available to provide care for older adults.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>What can you do?</h2>

<p>There’s likely no way to untangle decades of family dynamics before caretaking responsibilities kick in. But a few guidelines can help ensure that caregivers feel supported.</p>

<p><strong>Thinking ahead:</strong> Many caregivers in our focus groups felt thrown into their roles because their older friend or relative <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/15333175251357328">did not make plans for their care</a> in case their health were to fail. The lack of planning meant that caregivers were left to make decisions for the older adult, while worrying about whether they were <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/13607863.2015.1049117">adhering to their preferences</a>. Many caregivers <a href="https://doi.org/10.1332/23978821Y2025D000000166">found this incredibly stressful</a> – particularly as dementia’s progression makes it more difficult for people to make their wishes clear. </p>

<p>That’s why making plans in advance is vital – both for <a href="https://dementia-directive.org/">dementia specifically</a> and for <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/geroni/igx012">other types of health issues</a>. Preparation can include making <a href="https://theconversation.com/end-of-life-planning-can-be-hampered-by-misconceptions-but-the-process-is-easier-than-you-might-think-249265">legal arrangements</a>, such as healthcare directives and wills, as well as deciding who should provide care and what that care should entail. This is especially important for people who may <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.socscimed.2026.119251">not have family available</a> to care for them.</p>

<p><strong>Collaboration:</strong> Caring for a family member – particularly someone undergoing challenging cognitive changes and especially with tricky family history – may take a lot of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1471301218780768">negotiation</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/jpm.12822">communication</a> and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/jftr.70054">flexibility</a>. It is important to continue to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/14713012251389447">include the older adult in these conversations</a> even as their <a href="https://www.girlfridayproductions.com/titles/before-i-lose-my-own-mind">disease progresses</a>. </p>

<p>In our focus groups, caregivers said they most appreciated <a href="https://doi.org/10.1145/3555133">knowing they weren’t alone</a> in dealing both with caregiving and family dynamics. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/gerona/glae036">Respite care</a> and other programs, including <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/13607863.2023.2194848">support groups</a>, can give caregivers some time away. Families are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1186/s13690-018-0316-y">often unaware</a> of <a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/alz.70013">these programs</a>. These programs may also not be everyone’s cup of tea – perhaps due to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1332/23978821Y2024D000000059">cultural or personal values</a> around avoiding outside involvement.</p>

<p>If you are seeking outside support, start with your local <a href="https://ihpi.umich.edu/news-events/news/7-things-every-family-caregiver-should-know-many-dont">Area Agency on Aging</a>. These agencies are a network of <a href="https://eldercare.acl.gov/home">local nonprofit organizations</a> around the country that help connect older adults and their caregivers to resources, including help with meals, long-term care planning or accessing respite care.  </p>

<p><strong>Seeking community:</strong> Caregiving often involves <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.44315">supporting other caregivers</a>. For example, one participant in our focus groups noted that her efforts caring for her grandmother also supported her mother, whom she saw as the main caregiver. But because family dynamics and histories vary so widely, some care networks function cohesively <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/geronb/gbaf040">while others may struggle</a>. Support groups can help families connect with others <a href="https://www.mentalhealth.com/library/support-groups">navigating similar challenges</a>.</p>

<p>In addition, community engagement for people with dementia and their caregivers is increasingly widespread. Local <a href="https://www.dementiafriendlyservices.org/">“dementia friendly” programming</a> can provide outings and other activities, as well as another place to meet other caregivers similar to support groups.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/280415/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

I am a sociologist and demographer studying how family dynamics change as people get older and need care – and how that relates to expectations about caregiving for older adults
The makeup of families is changing, and that’s shaking up how caregiving can reverberate through family relationships
Caring for family members or friends with dementia can be especially thorny because of the ways the condition changes how a person behaves and how they interact with others
But a little planning and support can help families through the challenges
Caregiving is a common experience Americans are living much longer, which means that people are sharing more years of their lives with their family members
For instance, children are more likely to have a living grandparent today than in previous generations
And that means it’s more likely that people will have a parent or grandparent who may experience cognitive decline at some point in their lives
More than 5 million U.S. adults age 65 and older are currently living with dementia – an umbrella term describing a loss of cognitive abilities around thinking, remembering and reasoning
That number is expected to reach over 13 million by 2060 as the baby boomers age
Caregiving for people with dementia is a family affair
Flashpop/DigitalVision via Getty Images People with dementia interact with many people in their families and communities
Over half of Americans say that they know someone with dementia , and more than a third of extended families include an older adult with dementia
In 2022, over 5 million family caregivers were taking care of an older adult with dementia
That’s 1 out of every 5 people caring for an older adult in the U.S
At the same time, family sizes are shrinking, and more older adults do not have children or their children live far away – and more distance often equates to less caregiving
Meanwhile, cultural acceptance of the idea of family estrangement or going “no contact” has increased – as has a growing recognition of chosen family
That means more older adults are aging alone , with limited support, or with other people who may not have the legal benefits of immediate family
The caregiving landscape is shifting, too
Historically, middle-age women were the largest group of caregivers – generally, the daughters of aging parents
Adult children continue to be the largest group of caregivers for older adults with dementia in the U.S., but their characteristics are changing
Today, more caregivers are age 65 and older themselves
And more men , young people and friends are also providing care
All these factors combined are changing who is available to provide care for aging family members
Great expectations Dementia can amplify both expectations and family messiness

Using data from a survey conducted by the RAND Corporation, a nonprofit research organization, my colleagues and I found that Americans feel families have a greater responsibility to care for an older relative with dementia than for a relative with a physical illness
These expectations can motivate some caregivers to provide care, even in difficult circumstances
But for others, old family disagreements, rivalries or unresolved points of tension can continue to haunt relationships in ways that can clash with family expectations around caretaking
Dementia further complicates these feelings
For instance, one participant in our focus groups described a friend who struggled with caregiving because he felt compelled to do it even though his dad had not cared for him when he was a child
Shrinking families also leads to constrained options
Some caregivers report feeling they have no choice but to provide care, especially when the older adult has dementia
In our focus groups, this was often because no one else was available due to small family sizes or even family estrangement
Caring for someone with dementia often requires a large circle of support , leading to potential clashes between family members
In our focus groups, this played out as caregivers disagreeing on roles and responsibilities in ways that often reflected prior family tensions
Changing family structures are shaking up who’s available to provide care for older adults

<title>How the US gave up its edge to China in processing vital rare earth minerals – and what that’s costing</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761620/original/file-20260923-50-jokvci.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=797%2C948%2C4202%2C2801&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">MP Materials mines and processes rare earth minerals in California, including neodymium-praseodymium oxide used in high-performance magnets.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/in-an-aerial-view-the-mountain-pass-rare-earth-mine-north-news-photo/2270755803?adppopup=true">David McNew/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Look around you, and you’ll see rare earth elements at work. A phone vibrates because <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2018/10/18/neodymium-china-controls-rare-earth-used-in-phones-electric-cars.html">a magnet moves a weight</a>. Its screen was polished with cerium powder. Its connection to the rest of the world crosses oceans on <a href="https://hackaday.com/2023/08/08/under-the-sea-optical-repeaters-for-submarine-cables/">cables amplified with erbium</a>. If you drove today, a rare earth magnet helped you steer, and a <a href="https://profession.americangeosciences.org/collections/geoscience-faq/how-do-we-use-rare-earth-elements/">cerium compound scrubbed the exhaust</a>.</p>

<p>All of these devices function because of <a href="https://pubs.usgs.gov/fs/2014/3078/pdf/fs2014-3078.pdf">17 metals collectively known as rare earth elements</a>. The scientists who gave the group that name in 1794 created a misnomer. Cerium alone is about as common in the Earth’s crust as copper.</p>

<p>However, separating rare earth minerals from one another and from raw ore is intensely difficult. As a result, countries that control the processing of rare earth minerals have a lot of political leverage.</p>

<p>China processes most of the rare earth minerals used around the world, and it isn’t just consumer electronics that depend on Chinese exports. The U.S. military’s <a href="https://www.csis.org/analysis/consequences-chinas-new-rare-earths-export-restrictions">F-35 fighter jets and Virginia-class submarines</a> need rare earths too. </p>



<p>I spent years <a href="https://usnwc.edu/Faculty-and-Departments/Directory/Charles-Edward-Gehrke">adjudicating war games for the U.S. Navy</a>. War games force players to identify the hidden constraints that render a beautiful plan untenable. Rare earth processing is exactly such a constraint.</p>

<p>China showcased the power of its rare earths leverage with a <a href="https://www.pillsburylaw.com/en/news-and-insights/china-suspends-export-controls-certain-critical-minerals-related-items.html">series of export controls</a> issued in 2025 that it agreed to suspend – at least until Nov. 10, 2026. Controlling the supply enables a government to slow a rival’s growth, or halt it. China’s ability to extend the suspension of its export controls or let them go into effect gives it leverage on the geopolitical stage. In the parlance of Theodore Roosevelt, it’s a very <a href="https://www.theodorerooseveltcenter.org/quote/speak-softly-and-carry-a-big-stick-you-will-go-far-if-a-man-continually-blusters-if-he-lacks-civility-a-big-stick-will-not-save-him-from-trouble-and-neither-will-speaking-softly-avail-i/">big stick</a>.</p>

<h2>How China took the lead</h2>

<p>California’s Mountain Pass mine <a href="https://www.sciencenews.org/article/rare-earth-mining-renewable-energy-future">led world production of rare earths until the late 1980s</a>. Multiple instances of <a href="https://www.hcn.org/issues/47-11/why-rare-earth-mining-in-the-west-is-a-bust/">radioactive wastewater spilling from the mine into the Mojave Desert</a> made it hard to keep domestic production running.</p>

<p>When China expanded its own mining and sold the processed materials for less, the logic of switching rare earth suppliers was easy. </p>

<p>Mountain Pass’ <a href="https://www.gao.gov/assets/a96655.html">separation plant closed in 1998</a>, and the mine itself stopped in 2002. MP Materials <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/mp-materials-rare-earths-mine-us-china-trade-60-minutes/">restarted mining there in 2017</a> as concern about access to rare earth minerals rose, but the U.S. still <a href="https://pubs.usgs.gov/periodicals/mcs2026/mcs2026-rare-earths.pdf">imported more than two-thirds</a> of the rare earth elements it used as recently as 2025.</p>

<p>China, which mined about 60% of the world’s rare earth elements used in magnets in 2024, handled about <a href="https://www.iea.org/commentaries/with-new-export-controls-on-critical-minerals-supply-concentration-risks-become-reality">91% of separation and refining</a>. </p>

<p>Buyers using processing in China got material below the cost of making it themselves, and none of the cleanup bills or the bad press. But they ceded leverage to the processor in exchange. The trade was understood. It just didn’t look as threatening at first from a China that was still rising.</p>

<h2>Why rebuilding is slow</h2>

<p>The U.S. Government Accountability Office cited estimates in 2010 that rebuilding a domestic supply chain including mining, separation and magnet manufacturing would take <a href="https://www.gao.gov/assets/a96655.html">as long as 15 years</a>. Actually rebuilding that supply chain has been slow for several reasons.</p>

<p>China runs its plants with thousands of experienced engineers; the U.S. <a href="https://www.uts.edu.au/news/2025/11/why-the-west-cant-escape-chinas-rare-earth-dominance--yet">has far fewer experts</a>. Today’s industrial-scale cutting-edge technologies were developed in China, and the government there has no reason to share. Beijing also <a href="https://www.csis.org/analysis/what-chinas-ban-rare-earths-processing-technology-exports-means">banned exports of the separation technology itself</a> in December 2023.</p>

              <span class="caption">The U.S. has rare earth deposits, but little mining. The pink areas in this U.S. Geological Survey map are believed to have potential for rare earth deposits.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.usgs.gov/mission-areas/energy-and-minerals/news/maps-maps-maps-where-might-scientists-search-minerals">USGS</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>The U.S. government has committed more than <a href="https://www.csis.org/analysis/rare-earth-export-restrictions-one-year-later">US$7 billion</a> since April 2025 to try to rebuild U.S. rare earth production capacity. The Pentagon bought <a href="https://mpmaterials.com/news/mp-materials-announces-transformational-public-private-partnership-with-the-department-of-defense-to-accelerate-u-s-rare-earth-magnet-independence/">$400 million of preferred stock in rare earth producer MP Materials</a> in 2025, giving it 15% ownership of the company. MP Materials expects its next magnet plant to begin testing the equipment in 2028. </p>

<p>The Commerce Department also signed <a href="https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/01/department-commerces-chips-program-announces-letter-intent-usa-rare-earth">a letter of intent</a> in 2026 to give a magnet maker, USA Rare Earth, $277 million in direct funding and a $1.3 billion loan, both aimed at developing facilities in Texas and Oklahoma.</p>

<p>But export roadblocks put up by China are making rebuilding that supply chain more difficult.</p>

<h2>What happens on Nov. 10</h2>

<p>On Oct. 9, 2025, China’s Ministry of Commerce announced <a href="https://www.pillsburylaw.com/en/news-and-insights/china-suspends-export-controls-certain-critical-minerals-related-items.html">six wide-ranging export control measures</a>. One, Announcement No. 61, affects what even factories abroad can export. A factory in Germany or Japan would need a Chinese license to export a product if Chinese-origin rare earths made up <a href="https://www.china-briefing.com/news/chinas-rare-earth-export-controls-impacts-on-businesses/">0.1% or more of its value</a>, or if it used Chinese rare earth technology.</p>

<p>After President Donald <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2025/11/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-strikes-deal-on-economic-and-trade-relations-with-china/">Trump met Chinese leader Xi Jinping that month</a>, Beijing <a href="https://www.cirs-group.com/en/chemicals/china-temporarily-suspends-export-controls-on-key-raw-materials-including-rare-earths-lithium-batteries-and-diamond">suspended six export controls until Nov. 10, 2026</a>, in exchange for Washington pausing its “<a href="https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/11/12/2025-19846/one-year-suspension-of-expansion-of-end-user-controls-for-affiliates-of-certain-listed-entities">affiliates rule</a>,” which imposes restrictions on companies that are majority-owned by certain blacklisted firms, for one year. </p>

<p>Both controls snap back into place automatically unless both governments extend their pauses.</p>

<h2>What stays in place</h2>

<p>Some of the export rules were never suspended, including licensing imposed by China in April 2025 on exports of seven of the <a href="https://www.csis.org/analysis/consequences-chinas-new-rare-earths-export-restrictions">heavier rare earths</a>.</p>

<p>Automaker Ford saw how the export controls can affect a company when it had to idle its Chicago assembly plant for a week in May 2025 for want of magnets – critical to speakers and electrical motors – because of the export rules. Ford CEO Jim Farley described his supply as “<a href="https://fortune.com/2025/06/13/ford-ceo-says-rare-earth-supply-is-day-to-day-after-plant-halt">day to day</a>” because he had no alternate source. Ford was able to resume production <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2025/06/06/china-issues-rare-earth-licenses-to-suppliers-of-top-3-us-automakers-sources-say-reuters.html">only with Beijing’s approval</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761464/original/file-20260922-50-ozlbpw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A woman looks at large chunks of rock." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761464/original/file-20260922-50-ozlbpw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/761464/original/file-20260922-50-ozlbpw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=394&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761464/original/file-20260922-50-ozlbpw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=394&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761464/original/file-20260922-50-ozlbpw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=394&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761464/original/file-20260922-50-ozlbpw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=495&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761464/original/file-20260922-50-ozlbpw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=495&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/761464/original/file-20260922-50-ozlbpw.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=495&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A visitor stops by a rare earth iron ore exhibit during the 5th China-Mongolia Expo on Aug. 26, 2025, in Hohhot, China.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/woman-views-rare-earth-iron-ore-exhibit-during-the-5th-news-photo/2244098295?adppopup=true">Ding Genhou/VCG via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>On June 22, 2026, China’s Ministry of Commerce put <a href="https://www.cirs-group.com/en/chemicals/dual-use-exports-to-the-us-further-restricted-10-us-entities-added-to-chinas-export-control-list">10 U.S. companies on its export control list</a>. Neither Chinese nor foreign firms can sell those companies any goods that have both civilian and military uses. Most of them build drones, radar, aerospace systems and military vehicles. Two of them – MP Materials and USA Rare Earth – are the <a href="https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/01/department-commerces-chips-program-announces-letter-intent-usa-rare-earth">federally backed</a> American companies furthest along in building a mine-to-magnet chain.</p>

<p>Beijing said its move was <a href="https://www.globalsecurity.org/wmd/library/news/china/2026/06/china-260622-globaltimes02.htm">a response</a> to a <a href="https://www.wilmerhale.com/en/insights/client-alerts/20260611-pentagon-adds-65-new-entities-to-the-1260h-list-of-chinese-military-companies">similar move by the Pentagon</a>. My interpretation is that China picked MP Materials and USA Rare Earth because they are best placed to reduce America’s need for Chinese processing.</p>

<p>An extension of the pause on Nov. 10 would honor the truce, but the heavy rare earth licenses and the June 22 ban on the targeted firms would still apply. The truce means both parties get to play nice. It doesn’t mean they are being nice. </p>

<h2>Three paths</h2>

<p>For the U.S., leaving processing in China is the fastest and cheapest solution, but that leaves it <a href="https://source.benchmarkminerals.com/article/ex-china-rare-earths-premium-to-grow-especially-for-heavies">exposed to Beijing’s restrictions</a>.</p>

<p>Rebuilding a U.S. rare earths supply chain would remove most U.S. dependence on China for rare earths and the political leverage it implies. But it would take longer, startup costs run to the billions of dollars and separation produces <a href="https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1363891">acidic, and sometimes radioactive, residues</a>.</p>

<p>Building a supply chain with allies such as Australia or Japan, both of which have started to build capacity, would lower the risk of the U.S. being cut off unilaterally. <a href="https://www.weforum.org/stories/2023/10/japan-rare-earth-minerals/">Japan has run this play with some success</a>, but the suspended Chinese rules affect any use of their technology abroad.</p>

<p>President Xi’s <a href="https://asia.nikkei.com/politics/international-relations/us-china-tensions/trump-says-xi-will-visit-us-on-sept.-24">Sept. 24, 2026, meeting</a> with Trump may help determine the status of the Nov. 10 restrictions, but the larger conflict over leverage will continue.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292631/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

MP Materials restarted mining there in 2017 as concern about access to rare earth minerals rose, but the U.S. still imported more than two-thirds of the rare earth elements it used as recently as 2025
The U.S. has rare earth minerals, but few mines
For years, it shipped much of what it does mine overseas for processing

Buyers using processing in China got material below the cost of making it themselves, and none of the cleanup bills or the bad press
But they ceded leverage to the processor in exchange
It just didn’t look as threatening at first from a China that was still rising
Government Accountability Office cited estimates in 2010 that rebuilding a domestic supply chain including mining, separation and magnet manufacturing would take as long as 15 years
Actually rebuilding that supply chain has been slow for several reasons
China runs its plants with thousands of experienced engineers; the U.S. has far fewer experts
Today’s industrial-scale cutting-edge technologies were developed in China, and the government there has no reason to share
Beijing also banned exports of the separation technology itself in December 2023

title: Trump is bracing to lose his latest fight with the press
excerpt: President Donald Trump answers questions from reporters in the Oval Office on September 18, 2026. | Samuel Corum/Bloomberg via Getty Images This story appeared
body: President Donald Trump answers questions from reporters in the Oval Office on September 18, 2026. | Samuel Corum/Bloomberg via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here
A hearing on President Donald Trump’s White House press ban ended without a ruling this afternoon — an admittedly anticlimactic outcome, but one that will likely change very soon
The Trump-appointed judge in the case, Timothy Kelly, appeared skeptical of the administration’s arguments for banning CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House grounds last week
Kelly said he would rule “as soon as possible.” Until then, the ban remains in place.  By all accounts, Trump’s case is a feeble one

While the Justice Department attempted to argue on Wednesday that the three outlets’ reporting jeopardized national security, Trump himself kind of gave the game away last week when he said he had singled these organizations out over what he characterized as negative and inaccurate stories

The move sat poorly even with people and institutions you’d expect to be sympathetic to Trump: Fox News was one of several outlets that boycotted White House events this week to protest the ban, for instance.  And ahead of today’s hearing, Trump himself seemed primed to lose
In a Truth Social post on Monday, he promised he would “almost without question” appeal any decision against him

Go a little deeper This is all emblematic of how Trump has escalated his attacks on the news media in his second term: not just by insulting and demeaning the press, but also by weaponizing otherwise neutral-seeming rules
Every administration has policies that regulate who can access the White House grounds and under what conditions, for instance
But in early 2025, the White House took control of the press pool — the rotating group of reporters that frequently travels with the president — and soon sought to  exclude disfavored organizations

More insidiously, Trump has mobilized regulatory agencies like the Federal Communications Commission against his perceived critics, in some cases even threatening to revoke the licenses of local TV stations that air coverage and commentary he disagrees with.  While no licenses have actually been suspended, the FCC has mysteriously pulled some up for unscheduled review

And just the prospect of government retaliation has been enough to force some content off the air: Just two weeks ago, the late-night comedy host Jimmy Kimmel said his show wouldn’t air a scheduled interview with Texas Senate candidate James Talarico because of the FCC’s new scrutiny of political content.  This playbook isn’t a Trump original, as my colleague Zack Beauchamp has explained

In fact, weaponizing broadcast regulations was also a favored technique of former Hungarian Prime Minister (and infamous strongman) Viktor Orbán, who successfully used licensing rules and other bureaucratic technicalities to force independent media outlets into submission.  Likewise, revoking the press credentials of critical reporters has long been a favorite tactic of Russian President Vladimir Putin, Nico Perrino, the executive vice president of the nonprofit civil liberties group Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, said in a briefing on Wednesday: “These are things that are done by regimes that we do not want to emulate.”  Lest these comparisons get you down, however, recall that neither Hungary nor Russia has all the defenses that the US does
Defenses like, for example, an independent court system

One new survey finds that the percentage of singles with a must-have trait list they’re checking off has risen to a whopping 34 percent
Experts blame larger cultural changes, the rise of dating apps, and negative social media narratives

But you can fight back in your own dating life by letting your guard (and maybe your standards!) down a little bit.  Before you go… Did you know …there are more than 1,000 designated wildlife corridors in the US ?
