title: Can AI actually save lives?
excerpt: The question "Should I kill humans?" is projected onto a wall behind robot "Alfie," a Moral Choice Machine. | Arne Dedert/picture alliance via Getty Images If t
body: The question "Should I kill humans?" is projected onto a wall behind robot "Alfie," a Moral Choice Machine. | Arne Dedert/picture alliance via Getty Images If there’s one thing that Americans can unite behind, it’s anxieties over artificial intelligence

According to a recent NBC News/Decision Desk poll , 70 percent of adults say they are personally more worried than excited about the technology; it’s basically underwater in every area of society with one notable exception: its use in scientific research and medicine
Dhruv Khullar , a physician at Weill Cornell Medicine and writer at the New Yorker, that optimism is well-founded
Khullar uses AI tools in his own practice as a physician and writes about their advancements in the medical field
He says that “right now, at least, there’s a generally optimistic view of how AI will change healthcare going forward.” AI in medicine is nothing new
In 2024, the Nobel Prize in Chemistry was given to researchers who developed an AI model that enabled breakthroughs in predicting protein’s complex structures
As it becomes more ubiquitous, it’s also emerging as a resource for doctors to get second opinions and as a tool to take notes on patient-doctor interactions

On top of that, Khullar says, it might help unlock new medicines to treat diseases.  Khullar joined Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram to discuss the ways that AI is transforming drug discovery and research, as well as what it still can’t do
They also discuss how to think about AI’s potential in healthcare at the same time as top AI researchers are increasingly warning about the technology’s risk
Below is an excerpt of the conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
You’ve been thinking about lifesaving AI innovation
Has AI already started saving lives? I think it has
This is the fastest I’ve ever seen healthcare take up a new technology
Part of that might be that the healthcare system is so messed up that there’s an appetite for some type of change
It’s unaffordable, it’s inaccessible, it’s inconvenient, the quality is uneven
There’s at least a hope that AI is going to help with all of these things, and I think it’s already starting to make its way into the healthcare system
Now it’s our responsibility to figure out how to make the most of it without also promulgating some of the downsides
For those who are unaware, tell us how it’s working its way into the system
It’s helpful to categorize it into a few buckets, at least for healthcare.  The most rapid uptake, and I think the place that it’s already starting to make a difference, is on the administrative side
Many people who have gone to a doctor recently might have noticed that there’s an AI scribe that’s taking notes now
And people seem to really like it, at least so far

Doctors are able to look their patients in the eye in the way that they weren’t able to when they were poring over their computers and just typing what the patient was telling them.  The second big area is patient navigation

When is your next scan? When’s your next appointment? Do I need to take this medication on an empty stomach or not? There’s a huge opportunity for people, let’s say, who are diagnosed with a serious illness like cancer or heart failure to navigate the system more seamlessly.  The third big area that I’m really excited about is drug discovery
AI is making a huge dent in the early parts of drug discovery.  The last thing that I’m excited about and that I use every day when I’m in the hospital is [AI] as a second opinion
Now instead of having to get a consult or turn to a textbook, AI can be a very, very helpful clinical decision support
It’s not to say that I never consult someone, of course, but that first pass — I’m not sure what’s going on

What are some recent trials that might influence my decision here? Is there something I’m missing? Is there a test that I should be ordering that I’m not ordering? — all those types of things, they start to help with
The biggest chunk of this positive view of AI and medicine is drug discovery
Tell me more about how that’s going so far and how it might be going in a year, or five, or 10

I don’t want to leave this conversation and say that we’ve solved the cure for cancer because of AI, but I do want people to know that at least for the early stages of drug discovery — figuring out the very basic steps of is this an interesting molecule? Does it have potential biological applications? — AI is already very helpful for that.  They’re trying to take, basically, what is an infinite number of drug-like molecules that are theoretically possible to be drugs and they’re trying to match that to some disease that’s going on inside a human
And human biology is incredibly complex as well

There’s tens of thousands of genes, hundreds of thousands of proteins, trillions of cells, and you have to match a potential molecule to a potential target within a human.  In the past, a researcher might take years to study a disease or a biological pathway and figure out, okay, this protein seems to be involved
And actually, it might not be involved, it might be involved, it might be disrupted, but not be the causative agent

There’s a lot of uncertainty there, so now AI can take enormous amounts of data, and it can rank various potential targets that seem to be the most likely to be causing a particular disease and give you that short short list of potential targets that may have taken months or years in the past
So now you know what to attack, but you have to figure out what to attack it with

So you need a molecule, you need to generate a molecule that’s going to fit into that target or disrupt that target in some way.  Now again, AI can scour vast chemical spaces and give you a list of the things that seem to be most likely to be able to disrupt that target
And then it can actually help you generate that molecule in some cases.  So now we have the target
Now we have something that we’re going to attack the target with
And then you have to do something called lead optimization, and that’s the third thing

title: It’s not your imagination — dating has gotten way more combative lately
excerpt: Lisa Marie Wilson matched with a man on a dating app who claimed to be 5-foot-10 and to live on the beach
body: Lisa Marie Wilson matched with a man on a dating app who claimed to be 5-foot-10 and to live on the beach
Only one of those facts turned out to be true
When she showed up to the date, Wilson observed that she and her date were the same height — and she isn’t 5-foot-10
She wasn’t planning to mention it, but her date did: “He told me I wasn’t really 5-foot-9,” Wilson, a 51-year-old author, told Vox
Even though he accused her of lying about her height before he even said hello, Wilson told Vox she still gave the man the benefit of the doubt

But as they continued on with their planned walk along the beach, Wilson sensed her date was suspicious of her. “The whole time it was like he was an investigative reporter asking me questions, but kind of like if you were interviewing someone you didn’t like,” she said.  By the end of the date, Wilson was sure she didn’t want to see this guy again, so she turned down his offer to give her a massage and left

She couldn’t get past his accusatory comment about her height. “I was like, ‘I’m not a liar,’” Wilson said. “But I think he was — because he obviously wasn’t as tall as he was saying he was.” (To add insult to injury, Wilson’s date emailed her the next day breaking things off with her .) Why I reported this Lately I’ve noticed an outright antagonism among singles, online and off
They want to find love, but have been so burned by past relationships (or situationships) that they have a pessimistic view of dating
As a result, some singles cast blanket judgments about the very people with whom they hope to foster a relationship: They’re all bad
It turns out the reason why dating is so negative now is the pressure we put on strangers to fulfill our every fantasy, when that’s not how people have historically become attracted to one another

If you’ve been on a date recently, the phrase “love is a battlefield” might seem a fitting descriptor for the sordid state of romantic affairs.  According to this year’s Kinsey Institute Singles in America Survey , the percentage of singles with a “checklist” of what they’re looking for in a partner rose from 25 percent in 2021 to 34 percent in 2026
Dating has also become even more partisan this year, another survey found : A date’s political affiliation, especially if it conflicts with their own, is a major dealbreaker

This year, traditional gender roles and values have made a return , hardening some people’s idea of what romance looks like — a dynamic where a woman is pursued by a man with an absurdly strong jaw — and warping the expectations that women have of men and vice versa

Daters are also increasingly using AI to chat with matches on apps and bots’ infiltration of dating apps might have you questioning who you’re even chatting with in the first place.  It stands to reason that we’ve forgotten how to be human — and some of the basic rules of human decency — in our love lives
Relationship experts, historians, and critics agreed: Dating feels different now
A popular outlet for singles to share their gripes, the platform has given rise to new dating vernacular — rosters, breadcrumbing, goblintimacy

These new dynamics seeped into the dates themselves, with people openly antagonistic and confrontational from the jump.  Experts say that if your goal is to find love, or even just have a night of fun, assuming the worst of others — as so many seem to do right now — isn’t an effective strategy. “If you’re eternally suspicious, that tends to be a boundary to attraction,” Paul Eastwick , a psychology professor at the University of California Davis and author of Bonded by Evolution: The New Science of Love and Connection , told Vox.  The consequence of such hostility in dating is less tolerance — for ordinary friction, for learning lessons, for romance itself

So, what’s a single in 2026 to do? The problem with dating right now Most of modern dating followed a predictable pattern: Two singles met at church or at school or at work or at a party hosted by a mutual friend or through family

They might continue to see each other in social settings, gradually growing accustomed to one another’s personality, quirks, interests, until one person (usually the man, if they were straight) asked out the other on a date

Because they had mutual friends or coworkers in common, there was someone to vouch for them, to give some context to their life.  Since the early 2010s , the most popular way to meet a potential romantic partner has been through online dating
App users are exposed to swaths of people they might not have ordinarily met without having to leave the comfort of their homes, meaning they are going on dates with virtual strangers

The sussing-out phase — where your perception of a person grows from simply “hot woman” to “Amy, the funny blonde from my dodgeball team” — has been condensed or eliminated altogether. “It’s not like, I got to know this person naturally ,” Eastwick, also the co-host of the podcast Love Factually , said. “When somebody is a stranger, it’s maybe a little easier to come in with whatever negative assumptions you’ve gleaned from these online spaces.” Life as a whole in the US has become more combative and tense in the past decade, from political polarization to increasingly rude behavior
At work, our labor and time is extracted until we’re laid off ; at home, we’re suspicious of our neighbors
And dating is inherently vulnerable, rife with rejection and negative consequences.  Dating apps have played a huge role in this dramatic shift in tenor
While effective at connecting users with multiple eligible singles, apps don’t encourage slow-burn connections, which is how humans have historically grown attracted to one another

And when a date goes awry, terrible tales can be mined for engagement online, where commenters are quick to validate a unique experience as universal, often reinforcing gendered stereotypes, like “all men are toxic” and “all women are shallow.”   People have historically commiserated over their romantic lives as a way of bonding: Think of men in bars with their buddies bemoaning the old ball and chain, women lamenting their husbands not shouldering their share of household labor

During the feminist movement of the 1970s, women gathered to validate each other’s experiences and consider political responses to sexist issues, according to Rebecca Davis , a professor of history and women and gender studies at the University of Delaware

Social media now fulfills many of the same functions as these in-person conversations, Davis told Vox; people can take to TikTok or Reddit to share their frustrating or traumatic experiences, and comment sections are populated with others sharing their own similar stories
But unlike in the relatively private spaces of the past, these gripes now spread from individual to individual with little context, follow-up questions, or nuance
Algorithms reward extreme content and creators may embellish details to encourage engagement

Whether intentionally or not, TikToks about how coffee dates signify low effort and Reddit threads parroting misogynist language perpetuate harmful stereotypes. “People are good at finding a reason to externalize the difficulty of dating,” the writer Asa Seresin told Vox
It’s much easier to assume the people you date are altogether bad than it is to assess your own actions
In a viral essay published in 2019, Seresin gave the outward disdain with heterosexuality a name: heteropessimism
Since then, dating culture has only gotten more dismal, he said, in large part due to a national regression toward conservative views of gender and sexuality
Wade , contentious debates over transgender rights , and a generation of young men who believe a woman should obey her husband have become a dark cloud over the world of romance
Some of these more traditional beliefs have filtered into 33-year-old Brittni Kristine’s dating life
After only a few weeks of dating, a man Kristine had met on an app asked her to be exclusive, but his actions suggested he wasn’t fully invested

Whenever Kristine inquired about their plans for the week, the guy would get irritated. “His defense mechanism was essentially like, ‘Well, I didn’t tell you I wasn’t seeing you next week, so why would you assume?’” Kristine told Vox
Over the course of the month they dated, Kristine and the man got into multiple arguments of this nature until she’d grown exasperated with his stonewalling

His antagonism, Kristine suspected, stemmed from a puritanical view of sex and romance, where casually dating is seen as a moral failure. “I’ve had so many people tell me, ‘If I go on a first date with you and I find out that you have gone on another date in the past two weeks, basically I would never talk to you again because you’re promiscuous,’” she said

title: Trump gets a Greenland deal
excerpt: President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen sign a trilateral security deal on the sid
body: President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen sign a trilateral security deal on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York City on September 22, 2026. | Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump’s campaign to take over Greenland has reached a peaceful end — for now

What happened? Trump signed a new security agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland while at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, outlining an expanded US military presence on the island.  The deal is the result of months-long negotiations between the two countries and Greenland, which is a semi-autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark

Crucially, it reaffirms the “sovereignty and territorial integrity” of Denmark and Greenland, something Trump has spent the last year-and-a-half-plus threatening to sweep away.  What’s the context? Trump returned to office last year proclaiming that US “ownership and control of Greenland is an absolute necessity” for US national security, even though Denmark — and by extension Greenland — is a NATO ally.  That rhetoric quickly escalated, and by this January, Trump was suggesting that the US could even use force to take the island. “If we don’t do it the easy way,” he said — buying Greenland from Denmark, or perhaps bribing its residents to secede — “we’re going to do it the hard way.”  This, understandably, freaked Europe out, prompting multiple countries to deploy small numbers of troops to Greenland.  Does this mean Trump is done trying to take over? We can always hope

It’s possible Trump will claim this as a win and move on, even though Tuesday’s deal doesn’t fundamentally change the nature of the US-Greenland relationship. (Last week, he referred to it as “a dream come true” for the US.) That being said, Trump’s desire to own Greenland always made more sense as an attempted legacy move than anything else, whatever his professed justifications

So while he might be happy to take the win for now, with the war in Iran still on and the midterms fast approaching, it shouldn’t be surprising if he’s clamoring for ownership again before his term is up

And with that, it’s time to log off… Hi readers, happy fall equinox! In addition to the start of astronomical autumn, it also marks the recurrence of “Chicagohenge”: As this NPR story explains , for a few days each year, the sun aligns with the city’s rigidly gridded streets to create a stunning view. (It happens in other cities as well, but not always on the vernal and autumnal equinoxes.) Thanks for reading, have a great evening, and we’ll see you tomorrow!

title: The psychology behind Trump’s obsession with DC renovations
excerpt: The White House campus, including a new helipad on the South Lawn and President Donald Trump ballroom that’s under construction, are seen from above on Septembe
body: The White House campus, including a new helipad on the South Lawn and President Donald Trump ballroom that’s under construction, are seen from above on September 21, 2026. | Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images Since President Donald Trump returned to office, he has moved aggressively to leave his mark
Many of his most visible legacy projects are not pieces of legislation, though
They’re part of a campaign to reshape Washington, DC, itself.  Last year, Trump knocked down the East Wing of the White House to make way for his massive new ballroom
He tried renovating the Reflecting Pool, which did not turn out well
He regilded four large statues near the National Mall, paved the White House Rose Garden, and drenched the Oval Office in gold and golden appliqués

Other Trump plans are still in the works: He’s proposed building a 250-foot triumphal arch in a traffic circle between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, just across the Potomac River
He now says the arch would double as a “military complex,” housing drones, snipers, and ammunition

And, of course, there’s the ongoing fight over the Kennedy Center , which Trump has threatened could be “ripped down” if he doesn’t get his name on the building in some capacity (he already tried once, and was ordered by a court to remove it)
Luckily, Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke with New York magazine’s Ben Terris, who recently spent time with Trump touring the ballroom construction site
Terris explains what ties all the disparate projects together and what they reveal about the Trump’s effort to reshape the nation’s capital — and his own legacy
Below is an excerpt of the conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
What is up with Trump’s obsession with physical landmarks?  Before I even talked to him, I did a lot of reporting about why he seems to be so obsessed with all this stuff
And it’s really like a legacy for him
He’s trying to build something that will last beyond his time here, both his time here in the White House and probably his time here on Earth
He wants to actually have physical monuments to himself.  Somebody who’s close to him told me that the president doesn’t care that much about legislation
He doesn’t care that much about the kind of nuts and bolts of being a president
He cares a lot about buildings and prizes
If he has buildings and prizes, then he feels like his legacy will go on forever
That’s why he wants the Nobel Prize
That’s why he’s building an arch for himself in Washington
It’s really about a legacy that will withstand the test of time in his mind
Which is to say, he doesn’t really realize that the right legislation could get him more prizes
Most presidents try to be very successful presidents and have other people build monuments for you
He’s trying to honor himself, basically
It’s something I asked him about actually when I sat down with him in the Oval Office
There was a viral moment a few months ago from Senator Jon Ossoff, the senator from Georgia who may run for president
And he said at a rally that the president is building monuments to himself because he knows that nobody will do it when he’s gone
I asked the president this because I thought maybe he’d take a shot at Jon Ossoff or deny it, but I was very surprised
He just said, “Yeah, that’s true

When I’m gone, nobody will do it.”  It feels kind of self-aware, surprisingly, of Donald Trump to not take a shot at Jon Ossoff, but to just agree with him and say, “Yeah, that’s exactly my motivation.” Part of me though — okay, here’s a guy who recognizes that when he’s gone, history may not necessarily look fondly upon him
But also there was a part of me that thought that that’s not actually what he was saying
What he was maybe saying is, “I’m the only person in the world capable of building something as beautiful and important as these monuments
I alone can build it.” Nobody else has the ability to do this the way that he has
So on the one hand, possibly self-aware that he won’t be recognized the way he wants to be
On the other hand, maybe it’s just a kind of egomaniac talking about how he’s incredible at things and nobody else can do it

I think it’s all kind of tied up in that he’s not the most introspective person I’ve ever talked to, let’s put it that way.  But even the least introspective person in the world, when he gets to be 80 years old, might start thinking about what’s left of him after he’s gone
Tell me about the tour President Trump gave you.  I thought I was going to get 20 minutes with him in the Oval Office

I ended up getting 45 minutes in the Oval Office and then almost a 45-minute tour of the White House grounds.  He showed me the Rose Garden, where they put statues and they turned it into a kind of paved-over terrace that looks like Mar-a-Lago

He showed me the Presidential Walk of Fame, where they have all the pictures of the presidents and then the autopen for Joe Biden , and a room called the Palm Room where he put down a new marble floor that he was very proud of

title: The uncomfortable truth about aquariums
excerpt: Young visitors watch the beluga whales at L'Oceanogràfic in Valencia, Spain. | Miguel Candela/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images This story appeared in&nb
body: Young visitors watch the beluga whales at L'Oceanogràfic in Valencia, Spain. | Miguel Candela/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

Four beluga whales have died in a month at one of America’s top-rated aquariums — a tragic development and, arguably, a reason to revisit the ethics of zoos. (More on that in just a minute.) The latest cetacean casualty, a 26-year-old female named Osiris, died at Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium yesterday

She follows 34-year-old Beethoven, a longtime resident of the aquarium, as well as 20-year-old Rain and 23-year-old Peekachu, who died in late August and early September.    Osiris, Rain and Peekachu were all part of the Marineland diaspora: a group of four dolphins and 30 beluga whales that rescuers have worked to relocate since the 2024 closure of a scandal-plagued theme park in Niagara Falls, Canada
This summer, the animals were successfully transferred to aquariums and marine parks in the US and Spain

That was a frankly incredible undertaking involving padded shipping containers, a police-escorted convoy and a chartered plane.  But in some regards, the international flight wasn’t even the hardest part of the whales’ journeys

Some of the animals have struggled to thrive in their new environments — even when those environments are state-of-the-art, like Shedd.  In a blog post announcing Osiris’s death, the aquarium noted that its rescued whales had been under 24-hour supervision and receiving intensive, specialized care
The aquarium is still investigating the cause of death for all four whales.  Go a little deeper View Link Believe me when I tell you that it gives me no pleasure to write the following paragraphs

In fact, as a kid, I grew up visiting the now-shuttered and much-maligned Marineland.  But incidents like these back-to-back deaths should prompt us all to ask ourselves who aquariums and zoos are actually for

And the answer, I regret to tell you, is frequently not “the animals” — though zoos and aquariums have, since the mid-20th century, marketed themselves as both tourist attractions and important players in wildlife education and conservation.   As my colleague Kenny Torrella writes, these institutions and their defenders argue they protect animals in three ways: first, by raising money for wildlife conservation projects; second, by helping to reintroduce vulnerable species back into the wild; and third, by inspiring visitors to take an interest in the environment

The Shedd Aquarium’s motto, for instance, is “For Love of Waterkind.”  It’s worth scrutinizing those purported virtues, however — even when prestigious and reputable institutions like Shedd are making them

On one hand, there is merit to the claim that zoos and aquariums fundraise for wildlife conservation: In 2022, the latest year for which data is available, one group of accredited zoos and aquariums spent more than a quarter of a billion dollars on habitat projects.  The evidence is thinner on the other points, though
It’s incredibly rare for aquariums and zoos to reintroduce endangered species back into the wild — that’s very difficult to do
And surveys of zoo and aquarium visitors show that merely seeing a wild animal in a tourist setting doesn’t generally galvanize people on matters of welfare or stewardship

Living in captivity in that tourist setting, however, can be stressful (or worse) for the animals themselves.  But what would a humane alternative look like? Even if zoos and aquariums stopped catching animals in the wild, that would still leave many thousands who are injured, orphaned, born in captivity, or otherwise accustomed to human care.  When it comes to whales, one nonprofit advocacy organization is already working on an alternative: a 110-acre coastal sanctuary for “retired” whales
That project, however, is still a long way from completion
And in the meantime, it’s up to consumers to decide whether the stated benefits of zoos and aquariums outweigh the potential harms to the animals they exhibit
One link for later ➨ Beware the trap of “moral perfection.” We should all endeavor to live lives that embody our values, sure
But if you never board a plane because you care about the climate, or you never take your kid to zoos because you read the arguments above, then you might end up with a smaller, less-lived life

And that’s no good, either.  Before you go… Did you know …that there have been “revolutionary” advancements in Alzheimer’s treatments in just the past five years? Two new drugs both markedly slow the progress of dementia

body: Group trapped at Hotel Bamy after US removal as rights groups sound alarm over poor conditions and violence Two men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs, all in plain view of other US deportees, according to witnesses and human rights lawyers
